Mr. Chairman, at this stage in the study of the estimates of the Department of Justice, I should like to direct a few remarks to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) with regard to an act which is of concern to his department. I refer to the Bankruptcy Act.
Much is being said in the newspapers about the administration of that act, which has been in force since July 1, 1950, a period of 11 years.
Much is made of fraudulent bankruptcies. Representations have been made by all kinds of organizations, including the Canadian lumber association, with the support of the national retail lumbermen and the provincial wholesale association, in May 1961.
Those businessmen complain about various provisions of the Bankruptcy Act. They claim that transfers which are made within three months before a bankruptcy, and which are valid, should be extended over a period of two years. Others feel that no one should be allowed to go into bankruptcy unless indebted to an amount of at least $3,000.
Mr. Chairman, I feel the act should be improved. In fact, the time has come to
Supply-Justice
refer it to a committee of the house for consideration and for necessary admendments. However, if some amendments cannot be submitted to a committee before some time, it would certainly be possible to improve it in the meantime.
The situation is this. There are many complaints about fraudulent bankruptcies. There is no doubt some bankruptcies are fraudulent, and in that regard, the Canadian Bar Association, at a meeting held last winter in Quebec city, made certain recommendations to the Minister of Justice.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to protect the people who resort to fraudulent bankruptcies, and I suggest that to prevent such things, we should apply tighter controls in such cases.
What happens today is that some trustees go into remote districts where they consult credit agencies and suggest to the debtors that they file a petition for bankruptcy. The bankruptcy is not, in such cases, registered in the place of domicile of the bankrupt, but in the larger centres such as Montreal and Quebec, with the result that the creditors are not interested. If they are appointed as inspectors, they do not attend meetings because they live too far away from the place where the bankruptcy was registered. Then the goods described in the bankruptcy are carried away and sold elsewhere at ridiculous prices. The result is that the creditors get very little out of such sales.
I feel that if the act were amended in such a way as to force the bankrupt to register his assignment of property at his place of domicile, a great deal of fraud would be avoided.
Now, the Canadian Bar Association has also made a very useful suggestion, namely that:
An assistant superintendent of bankruptcy be appointed for each province to follow the procedures more closely and to ensure that assets be converted to the advantage of the creditors.
We must admit that the superintendent of bankruptcy, whose office is in Ottawa, is much too far from the places where bankruptcy petitions are filed.
The appointment of an assistant superintendent for the province of Quebec would already be an improvement.
But we should not mention only the person who is bankrupt; there are also voracious creditors who are always in a hurry and who could just "eat up" the debtor.
I have here a brief submitted by the credit granters' association of Canada where it is requested that the chapter of the Bankruptcy

Supply-Justice
Act dealing with small debtors whose debts do not amount to much, be amended especially as far as summary administration is concerned.
I would not state this categorically, but I am quite sure that unscrupulous finance companies are sponsoring the amendment proposed by the association.
Recently creditors have sold all kinds of furniture to businessmen in the Montreal district. They are in a hurry to file a bankruptcy petition.
Now, we know that under the Bankruptcy Act no petition may be withdrawn without leave of the court.
As I was saying, there are at present in the Montreal district a certain number of bankruptcy petitions. Every week someone comes before the court to ask that a petition be withdrawn. In other words, the Bankruptcy Act is being used to collect debts.
Now, before we scratch out the chapter on summary administration, I feel we should get rid of that epidemic of salesmen.
I will give you a few examples, for instance, that of the knitting machine salesmen. The Minister of Justice must certainly be aware of the case since the knitting machine industry has moved from Montreal to Vancouver to continue its highly suspicious work.
Here is how those people operated. They would sell a knitting machine for $400, give knitting lessons to the purchaser and undertake to buy any article the latter knitted. One fine day, the purchaser would find out that the salesmen had disappeared into thin air.
Before they left, however, they had been very careful to sell their sale contract to finance companies which undertook to collect any balance owing.
What could those unfortunate debtors do except file a petition in bankruptcy triggered by unscrupulous people?
There has been another racket involving salesmen of machines to manufacture milk powder. It was being carried on mostly in the province of Quebec. After they had made a sale the salesmen undertook to buy the milk powder. In the meantime they transferred the note to a finance company to look after the collection, and they dropped out of sight.
Finance companies are frantic. Most of them are loan shark outfits fattening on refunds paid out weekly by labourers. If 200 or 300 labourers have contracted to make those weekly payments, just multiply that figure by $5, and you will see that these companies are doing pretty well.
I am not prepared to admit, like the granter's association, that the whole chapter
[Mr. Meunier.l
on summary administration should be removed from the Bankruptcy Act, because we must get rid of those unscrupulous and greedy creditors.
Those are the only remarks I wanted to make. I hope that the minister will take them into consideration.
I hope too that he will not be content to listen to the grievances of large companies but will also heed representations of low wage earners, who are fairly often the victims of unscrupulous operators.
I should like now to deal with another matter, this one of current interest which was raised yesterday in Montreal. It is about the right of a defendant to be tried and heard in his own language.
Of course, I should not make a plea in favour of the individual in question, Pierre Biernacki, who is now before the court.
However, it seems to me that the R.C.M.P. did behave in a despicable way towards the accused. They knew that he could speak and understand French better than English. Yet he was charged and examined in English and directed to make confessions in that language.
Justice Lazure, whose efficiency and integrity are well known, admonished the R.C.M.P. yesterday, stating that it is the right of an accused to be tried by his fellow-men in the language of his choice.
I hope the minister will make a few comments on the matter after having seen this morning's papers.
I feel I must add that there are many French speaking R.C.M.P. officers in Montreal, as there are no doubt in the rest of the country.
We should see to it that such a situation does not happen again, even though the accused is a national of another country.

With respect to the matter of interpreters, my recollection is that I have been advised that Mr. Biernacki was asked several times if he wished to have an interpreter or the services of an interpreter and he indicated that he did not desire an interpreter, that he understood fully what he was being asked and did not wish to have the whole thing done through an interpreter. Even if Mr. Biernacki was provided with an interpreter, I was told that he is more fluent in French than in English, having started learning English only after he came to Canada.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that at least the bills of indictment could have been made out in French and that his admissions could have been taken down in French, since that is the language he talks best. I feel it would have been the natural thing to do.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the hon. member for Papineau a question based on his remarks.
He raised the matter of summary administration, suggesting that this procedure too often favoured the activities of loan sharks at the detriment of low wage earners.
Would the hon. member tell us if he is in favour of abolishing assignment and summary administration in so far as it brings us back to assignment of property as contained in the civil code of the province of Quebec?
At the same time, could he tell me whether, in his opinion, judges are not overly given to the practice which consists in letting debtors go free after six months when they have sought protection under the procedure known as summary administration or assignment of property, in cases where trustees take the initiative of preparing such summary administration or such assignment and ask that the debtor be allowed his freedom at the end of six months, where the sums involved are not very large and where creditors dare not oppose the move because the expense would be too high?

The hon. member's question is quite long. I take it he does not favour deletion of the chapter on summary administration from the Bankruptcy Act.
My remarks had to do with the Bankruptcy Act in general and the chapter on summary administration in particular.
I also said that we should not always listen to grievances put forward by large finance companies, associations and societies, but also take into consideration the poor and the lowly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a couple of problems to raise with the minister, but before doing so let me say this. I am not a lawyer and have no legal training. I did, however, check with the constitutional lawyer concerning the responsibilities of the Minister of Justice in his capacity as Attorney
Supply-Justice
General of Canada to give legal advice to all departments of government in relation to changes in legislation. The minister's responsibilities include some of the duties which I thought were his, and his role as Attorney General of Canada is not as barren of responsibility as some hon. members may believe. I refer, of course, to the dual role of the minister and the degree of dexterity that is demanded of him in performing two separate functions simultaneously.
I wish to refer to the case of a Riceville farmer, Gerald Rowe, against whom action was taken some time ago under the provisions of the Live Stock Pedigree Act. On a number of occasions the minister has been asked to grant a new trial or to take other action in his capacity as Attorney General of Canada.
I will quote briefly from an editorial published in the Glengarry News. The first portion of the editorial refers to the bill of rights and may not be relevant to this case. The editorial reads in part as follows:
Equality before the law and the protection of the law were the chief aims of Magna Carta back in 1215 when men who felt oppressed struck for freedom of the individual, no matter his station in society.
These individual rights must be guarded by each of us, we were thinking last week end after a talk with a Riceville farmer who for six years has been fighting to have what he considers an injustice against his person redressed. Periodically through those years Gerald Rowe, of Riceville, has been in to tell us of his troubles and his efforts to have what he considers a wrongful court conviction corrected.
I think all hon. members of the committee are familiar with the details of this case, which are set out in the editorial. A later paragraph reads:
He has spent thousands of dollars since seeking evidence that would refute the testimony offered against him at the trial. He has had a lengthy brief prepared by a lawyer and it purports to show evidence against him was not well founded. Mr. Rowe has approached Prime Minister Diefen-baker, Premier Frost, justice Minister Fulton, Ontario chief justice Dana Porter and many other public figures in an endeavour to have his case reopened. All his efforts have proved fertile-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am sorry; the word is "futile". I continue:
Mr. Rowe is convinced that the legal profession in Ontario has closed ranks against him. His lawyer was paid a retainer to appeal the conviction, he declares, and let the time for appeal elapse without taking necessary action. According to Mr. Rowe he has since contacted a number of solicitors who, for reasons unknown, failed to take proper steps in the case. The law society of upper Canada promised him an inquiry, he says; but nothing has come of it.
This is the feature of the Rowe case we like least. Here is a man who must be convinced he

has been treated unjustly by the law, else why would he be still striving six years later to clear his name. And in his efforts-

the hon. member can relate the case he is talking about to the estimates of the Department of Justice. As I indicated yesterday, the administration of justice is a matter of provincial jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This is the point; what Your Honour has said is not quite true. The administration of justice does fall within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice, I am advised by constitutional lawyers. On the point of order Your Honour has raised I wish to read a letter written to the minister by my leader's executive assistant under date of November 15, 1960, the relevant portions of which are as follows:
Mr. Rowe's case appears to be unusual since his desire to appeal his case seems to have been subverted by the action or lack of action of his own solicitors. Now, as you have pointed out, your power under section 596 of the Criminal Code is insufficient to allow you to order a new trial in this case.
Could you not, therefore, consider bringing in an amendment to the Criminal Code which would allow you to grant a new trial to Mr. Rowe and to others like him who have been convicted on summary conviction?
The reply of the minister written in his capacity as Attorney General of Canada under date of November 29, 1960, is as follows:
Thank you for your letter of the 15th instant recommending an amendment to section 596 of the Criminal Code to include convictions in proceedings by way of summary conviction as well as by way of indictment.
The last paragraph reads:
While I am not satisfied that Mr. Rowe's case would, in itself, warrant such an amendment you may be assured that your suggestion will receive most serious consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would permit the hon. member to discuss the proposed amendment, but certainly not to bring in a case that has nothing to do with the proposed amendment. That is the view I take of the situation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had no intention of discussing the case. It is quite a lengthy case, and I had no intention of discussing it. I was only reading this editorial, which does not discuss the case itself but only the legal aspects of it and the fact that this gentleman cannot obtain a retrial. I should like to read the last portion of this editorial in the Glengarry News:
This is the feature of the Rowe case we like least. Here is a man who must be convinced he has been treated unjustly by the law, else why would he be still striving six years later to clear his name. And in his efforts for a new hearing over the years he has come to feel the legal profession has closed ranks to prevent any chance of a retrial. His feeling is that those involved

now know they erred in convicting him, but that the legal profession and the courts prefer to cover up, rather than admit a mistake was made.
That is not a healthy belief for even one individual to hold in a society which proclaims the equality of all before the law.
We hold no brief for Mr. Rowe. We know nothing of the complexities of this case, but we have read his brief and we think the attorney general should study it again. Much better that the province incur the expense of a new trial rather than that one citizen be left with the conviction the law and the courts are set against justice being done.
What I am curious about, Mr. Chairman, is why the minister will not make this change which would allow an appeal to be heard. An appeal would be possible if this case had been proceeded with in any court other than a court of summary jurisdiction. I am told that if the case had been tried in any other court there would have been a much greater possibility of this man appealing his case.
The request has been made of the government within the last few weeks that there be a retrial in this case because new evidence can be produced and presented to the court. It seems to me all people should be given the opportunity to proceed through the due process of law in a manner which will obtain justice for them, and it seems to me the fact that a lawyer himself may have made a mistake should not prevent justice being given in any particular case.
Is it not within the power of the minister to allow this to be done? I have been told by those who are conversant with the law that the reason this course is followed is that otherwise litigation would be carried on over a period of years; you would never know when you had settled a case or whether you were ever going to settle it, if it could be reopened at any time. I have been told that there must be limits upon the time for appeal. However, in this particular case the crown was involved, and I should think even a person convicted of murder, or an offence which carried a sentence of life imprisonment should at any time during the course of that sentence be able to appeal for a new trial because new evidence had been produced.
The lawyer who prepared the brief is of the opinion that sufficient new evidence is available to warrant a reopening of the case, but under section 596 of the Criminal Code, which is the section covering this matter, at the present time the minister has not the right to reopen this case. It seems to me that some consideration could be given to changing the law itself, or this section of the Criminal Code, to allow those persons convicted in a court of summary jurisdiction, particularly in a case which affects the crown directly and where the crown is the only party involved, to proceed and either be proven guilty or have the case dismissed.

This case has also been taken to the remission branch. I have considerable correspondence that has taken place over the years where the remission branch has been involved. The farmer has been asked to go to the remission branch where he can appeal for a pardon. This is not satisfactory to the farmer, who does not want to be pardoned for something he feels he has not done. All he wants is what he considers to be justice. Farmers, like myself, not understanding the finer points of law, see no reason why they should not have the opportunity to prove their innocence. It should be noted in this case-as in many others, I presume-that the farmer knew he was not guilty and did not believe he had to prove that he was not guilty. He thought someone had to prove that he was guilty. It seems to me that he is now willing to prove he was not guilty because he found that he would be convicted if he was not willing to prove that in the first place.
I think the minister could give some consideration to at least clemency in those cases which he reviews himself and decides have some merit. I know the minister is not too sympathetic in this case. I know he had the R.C.M.P. throw this farmer out when he came to ask him to intervene in his case.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I did not change my mind, Mr. Chairman. I have said this is what I was told, and that is a fact. The minister says it is not true. I accept his word for it, and therefore it is not true. But I still have been told it is, and I do not think I have to withdraw that.
There is another matter I should like to raise. It is something the same as the previous matter. I think it comes within the jurisdiction of the minister in that he administers the legal aspects of the act, chapter 15 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1952. This matter relates to negotiable instruments. In this case I ask the minister whether he will give consideration to changing the right of people to transfer negotiable instruments from one company to another, and the difficulties that arise from this practice.
I have a case in mind which happened in my own riding. A woman had bought one of these knitting machines. The machine was unsatisfactory; it was not as represented. Accordingly she sent the knitting machine back, but shortly afterwards she received a letter from a collection agency. It is headed "Without Prejudice" and reads as follows:
Ee: Sentinel Credits-$330.00.
We enclose for your perusal a mimeographed copy of an article published in the Toronto Daily Star, February 2, 1961. Your position seems to be exactly the same as the defendant's in that case.
We have been assigned your promissory note. What you did with the merchandise after signing this promissory note is of no consequence to us.
We will accept weekly payments on the complete balance or a cash settlement on a reduced balance.
If you wish to prevent a costly court action (followed, after judgment, by a garnishee of your wages and/or bailiff action), contact this office immediately with your offer of settlement. We would like to help you save court costs and interest.
This letter is put out by the Sentinel collection agency, described as a division of the Sentinel Credit Corporation Limited, Toronto.
There are many things wrong with this letter. In particular it seems to imply that were the case to come before a court the decision could only be in favour of the collection agency, the defendant having to pay

Supply-Justice
costs and other legal expenses. The letter refers to an article which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star on February 2, 1961, and I should like to put this article on record. It is headed: "Knitting Machines-It Wouldn't Work, Must Pay Anyway."
A couple who claimed they didn't pay for a knitting machine they bought because "it was rusty, the needle was bent and it wouldn't work" has to pay for it anyway.
Judge H. W. Timmins ordered Mr. and Mrs. Dymitro Haluk of Windermere Ave., to pay $380 owing on the knitting machine to the Diamond Discount Corp. Ltd.
The finance company was suing the Haluks for that amount, claiming on February 10, 1957, the defendants had signed a promissory note in favour of the now defunct Trans-World Machine Co., Spadina Ave. for $360. The defendants never paid the note, now held by the finance company, the plaintiffs claimed.
The plaintiff company were asking the court for the $360 principal of the note, plus interest at 1 per cent a month from April 10, 1959.
Mrs. Jeannie Haluk told Judge Timmins she and her husband bought the machine after the Trans-World Machine Co. salesman told them they could knit socks and sweaters on it and the company would buy back the knitted products at 25 cents an ounce. She said when the machine arrived, it wasn't the one they ordered, that it never worked and even a teacher from the company couldn't make it work.
Mrs. Haluk said she and her husband finally returned the machine to the company.
I suggest to the Minister of Justice that we should take some action in Canada to protect people who buy merchandise and then find that the promissory note they signed has been transferred as a negotiable instrument to a second party which has no obligation to cover the warranty or extend any of the protection which would have been given, or should be given, if the note had remained in the hands of the first party. In other words, the sale of this note eliminated the rights of the buyer. I think some consideration should be given to changing the provisions which govern instruments of this type.

It may be late to raise a point of order, Mr. Chairman, but we have been listening to the hon. member discuss this question for some time, and surely it is essentially provincial in nature. It deals entirely with the rights of a holder of a negotiable instrument or a conditional sale agreement. This whole field is under provincial jurisdiction. It has nothing to do with the functions of this committee and, surely, nothing to do with the estimates of the Minister of Justice. It has no place in a discussion of these estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay unduly the passing of the first item of the estimates of the Department of Justice, but before the committee does pass that item, I should like to point out an individual case referred to me by a Toronto correspondent. While it is an individual case, it might concern everyone, since it has to do with an amendment to the Criminal Code.
Mr. Chairman, we all know that a person prosecuted on an indictable offence may, under section 508 of the Criminal Code, appeal to the presiding judge of the court for what is known as a change of venue. In fact, that section provides that a change of venue can be granted by the presiding judge, if he decides that it is to the best interest of justice. And we realize that the interest of justice means, not only the interest of society, but also the interest of the accused who is entitled to a complete and thorough defence.
As I said a moment ago, section 508 applies to cases of indictable or criminal offences which can be submitted to a jury. But it is entirely different, as far as I know, in the case of a trial before a judge only, either before or after the preliminary hearing, or when proceedings are taken under part 24 of the Criminal Code concerning summary convictions.

Now, the case submitted to me may be summarized as follows: if an accused, say from Montreal, is charged with an offence committed in Vancouver, after which he has returned to Montreal, he must necessarily appear in court in Vancouver. Is it possible, at present, for that accused to apply for a change of venue, that is to say, can he request to stand trial at the place of his domicile? I do not think so. This might be advisable in less serious cases, especially in cases of summary conviction.
At present, it is easy for an accused from Montreal to avoid being at a hearing in Vancouver; in such a case the crown would submit ex parte evidence, in the absence of the accused who would obviously be convicted on some charge and sentenced to pay court fees.
Now, if this accused has an excellent defence and is unable to go to Vancouver because he cannot afford the railway fare between Montreal and Vancouver, how can he submit a defence under the present system? I do not think anything provides for that case in the Criminal Code. I would like to make a few suggestions in this connection.
The officials of the department might perhaps look into this matter of distance, in the administration of the act.
Besides, they might consider the possibility when the crown proceeds according to part 24 of the Criminal Code; that the crown states its case in Vancouver and the record, including the reporter's transcript, could be transmitted in some way to Montreal where the accused could present his defence before a magistrate. Later on, the record could be returned to the place where the charge originated, and the judge who heard the first part of the evidence could then pass judgment.
This procedure might not be too satisfactory in the case of an accused who decides to enter a plea of not guilty. But I believe it would be wise to amend the Criminal Code to provide for the acceptance of a written plea of guilt in cases of summary conviction, as they are commonly called.
I do not know what is the traditional procedure in other provinces. Nor do I know whether in such cases, judges in Quebec city and in Montreal accept written pleas of guilt, but I know that in the rural areas of my province, the judges often accept such pleas.
Supply-Justice
In order that an individual, who is indicted and brought to court, may be saved considerable expense for the only purpose of personally recording a plea of guilty, a clerk of the court and the judges accept written pleas of guilty, and the presiding magistrate or judge returns his judgment in the absence of the accused, thus saving the cost of an enquiry.
Therefore, I would ask the minister to submit these few remarks to his legal advisers in order to determine the advisability of amending the Criminal Code to that effect, and more particularly part 24 of the Criminal Code.

Mr. Chairman, I understand the hon. member for Skeena made reference the day before yesterday to a conference which the minister held with the provincial attorneys general regarding the procedure to be devised for amending our constitution in Canada. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not replied in respect of that point.

The minister has held very important conferences with the provinces regarding this matter and, outside of the answers to one or two questions addressed to him during the course of this session, one asked by myself, there has not been, to my knowledge, any discussion in this house of this matter. Before the minister concludes his statement I think he should give us a report regarding the situation as it is at the present time.
As I understand it, there was a disposition on the part of most of the provinces, if not all, to try and find some modus operandi to provide for unanimous agreement between the provinces and the federal government in the matter of amendments to our constitution, and the placing of the power to amend with the proper legislative authority, or the proper legislative and executive authority, or authorities, here in Canada.
There are, of course, matters which concern the federal government and the provincial governments together in respect of constitutional amendments. There are matters which concern the provincial governments alone, and other matters which concern the federal government alone. We are not concerned with respect to those latter matters, but with those matters that concern both provincial and federal governments. I am sure there is an almost universal desire in our country that Canada should have the power to amend the Canadian constitution without resorting to another legislative body outside Canada. All that stands in the way of this is agreement between the two senior levels of government. It would be appreciated if, some time before this first item is concluded, the minister could give us indication as to what the situation is. As I understand it there was put forward by the spokesman for the province of Quebec, Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, a formula which seemed to be satisfactory to most of the provincial governments and the federal government. It would be interesting to hear from the minister in this connection.
I should also like to bring the minister's attention to another matter regarding the first item of his estimates. What progress has been made by the Minister of Justice particularly in the examination of all existing statutes which are thought by the law officers of the crown to be in any way inconsistent with the provisions of the bill of rights? During the discussion in the house prior to the enactment of the legislation it was argued that the bill of rights did not in any way add to our substantive law; that it was no more than declaratory of the existing law and that, in any event, some of its provisions would be found to be inconsistent with some of the existing statute law of Canada. It was further argued in this context, notwithstanding the contention made, notably by the Prime Minister, that the bill of rights would not supersede any inconsistent measure. It was pointed out by the Canadian Bar Association in the committee on the bill of rights that the bill would be inconsistent with certain legislation, notably the Immigration Act, and that the bill of rights itself would not remove that inconsistency notwithstanding the provision declaring that certain legislation inconsistent with the bill of rights would have the effect of causing those inconsistent enactments to be inoperative.
It is my feeling that this matter is still not clearly settled juridically, and the minister ought to give us some report. What steps have been taken by the administration to remove any anomalies or inconsistencies between the existing statute law and the bill of rights? Certainly nothing has been done by the administration thus far to indicate that it is prepared to bring forward amendments to any existing statutes to bring those statutes into conformity with the bill of rights.
We were told last session, for instance, that the War Measures Act would be amended in a manner to make it consistent with the bill of rights. It was strongly argued by the Minister of Justice last year that the amendments to the War Measures Act should not be made part of the bill of rights; that hon. members could be assured that that was in a sense a separate matter, and that it would be dealt with by the administration separately at the next session of parliament. The next session of parliament referred to at that time is this session, the end of which we are looking forward to and anticipating, but no measure has been brought forward by the government to amend the War Measures Act.
Indeed, there stands in my name now a private bill to amend the War Measures Act, which would make that act consistent with
(Mr. Fulton.]

the concepts and provisions of the bill of rights. If the government proposes to allow a measure introduced by a private member to do what it said itself it woul do, of course I have no objection. The important thing is to make sure that the War Measures Act and all other enactments do in fact conform with the spirit, the legal implications and directions of the bill of rights.
The third matter I should like to mention has to do with an announcement made by the minister during the course of the present session. It involves both his own administration and that of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and has to do with the treatment of drug addicts. The minister might indicate whether he proposes to bring down any legislation in that regard. I do not know whether the legislation to which he referred the day before yesterday in regard to barbiturates is to be regarded as more of an omnibus measure than the mere announcement vould indicate.
In any event, it would be interesting to know what progress has been made by the government in its discussions with the provinces with regard to the treatment centres contemplated. What does the government propose by way of additional legislation? Does it propose to increase the penalties for illicit drug addiction? Does it propose to take powers that would enable the crown to keep in confinement users of drugs who have violated the Criminal Code or the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, thereby taking advantage of the confinement to give those individuals the opportunity to be rehabilitated in a government institution? Is the institution the government has in mind something along the lines of that in Lexington? This is the only major institution of its kind where those administering the criminal law and those administering the health services in the United States combine in providing for detention and rehabilitation.
This is a matter of the greatest importance. What progress has been made in this regard? Since the greatest concentration of drug addicts is in the province of British Columbia, has some arrangement been made with that province, or does that province wish to pursue this course all by itself? What is the situation with regard to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec? I mention these three provinces particularly because, second only to British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec represent the areas where the greatest amount of drug addiction is found.
Before this item is passed, perhaps the minister will give us some indication of his reaction to what I have said.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will deal with the remarks of all those who have spoken this morning. The hon. member for Papineau brought to my attention some views with respect to the Bankruptcy Act. Those views have been noted accordingly. As the committee knows, we are in the course of a study of the Bankruptcy Act, and I am grateful to the hon. member for the expression of his opinion, which we will note carefully and consider in the course of that study.
The remarks of the hon. member for Timis-kaming will be given the consideration they deserve.
The hon. member for Megantic brought to my attention his views with respect to section 508 of the Criminal Code as to the desirability of making some provision for those situations where it is not possible, or at best extremely difficult and expensive, for an accused to get to the place where the trial is set, and also with regard to the question of entering a written plea of guilty. We will

Supply-Justice
consider both these matters. We had not included them in the Criminal Code amendment bill tor this year but we will certainly consider them for the future.
The hon. member for Essex East asked me for a progress report with respect to the conference of attorneys general for the purpose of devising a recommendation as to an acceptable method of amending the constitution in Canada. In answer to that inquiry, which was also made by the hon. member for Port Arthur two days ago, I should say that the last meeting of the attorneys general was held here in Ottawa in January of this year- our third meeting. A good deal of progress had been made toward arriving at an agreement among the attorneys general on a formula that we would feel we could recommend to our respective governments for consideration by them and, if approved, for submission by them to their respective legislatures and the parliament of Canada.
May I emphasize again, because I think it is important, that we are not a plenary body. We were instructed by our governments at our suggestion to meet in order to see if we could devise a formula which we would be prepared to recommend to those governments. I say that because there has been some suggestion that we are rushing things, and that the country will suddenly be confronted with a proposal emerging from our conference which will become the law. I know my hon. friend has not made that suggestion, but it has been made in other quarters and I wanted to lay it at rest.
I certainly hope that a proposal will emerge from our conference that will be acceptable to all governments and to the legislatures and parliament. That is our objective; but it is only after, first, the governments have studied our proposal and, second, the legislatures and parliament have approved any proposal we may make, that it would become effective. As I say, up to January a good deal of progress had been made. Unfortunately I cannot say that there was unanimity, but there was a very close approach to unanimity in so far as views could be ascertained at that time on a formula which had been worked out, amended and approved and worked up, as it were, as a result of the meetings and exchanges of views that we had had.
In January the suggestion was made and accepted by the attorneys general that we had now come about as close to agreement as we could usefully come at the conference and that what should happen was that the government of Canada, accepting the responsibility of putting into draft form what appeared to be the concensus emerging from the discussions, should undertake to prepare

a further draft on that basis and circulate it to all governments. It was then hoped that without the necessity of a further meeting the governments could consider that draft and indicate their views; and, as I say, it was hoped that the indication would be that it was acceptable. For what reason I am not certain, but this did not prove to be the case.
A draft was prepared accordingly and circulated by me but we heard from only a very few provinces as to their reactions to that proposal. I was in touch with them or with various of them on at least two occasions, I believe, but it appeared that, while none of them expressed any fundamental disagreement with the draft, they had become so engaged with their legislative sessions the matter was not dealt with as we had hoped it would be.
I came to the conclusion recently, therefore, that in order to ensure finality and, I trust, agreement it was desirable to reconvene another session of the conference of attorneys general. We had hoped to be able to conclude our work by correspondence, but in my view it has become evident that this will not be possible and that a little further impetus must be given. Therefore, within the last two weeks I have written again to each attorney general reminding him of the situation and saying that, since in my view it would be unfortunate if the impetus that had been gained and the results that were, we felt, so imminent of realization should be lost by lack of follow through, I was therefore suggesting that we meet again in the month of June or, if that were found not to be convenient, in the month of September, and I asked them to indicate their views as to a suitable date. Whenever we meet I hope we shall be able to arrive at a satisfactory conclusion to report back to our governments.
Does the minister feel that he can indicate which provinces did not concur in the general formula, or does he feel that he should not do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I feel that I should not at the moment. As I say, I have not had definite replies from any of them. Indeed, I had answers from only one or two provinces. One in particular, which will be as well known to my hon. friend as it is to me, made public its attitude toward the proposal being discussed. There is no secret about it; it was the province of Saskatchewan. They have not rejected it, but apart from their views the views of the others were very close to complete agreement. I might say that a number of provinces made proposals and put forward drafts, and we also put forward drafts

from time to time. Then we had the draftsmen work up what appeared to be the nearest concensus of the views expressed at which we could arrive.
The hon. member raised a question as to the extent to which my department has proceeded to study all the statutes of Canada with a view to bringing them into conformity with the bill of rights. I have to remind the hon. member that at the time of the discussion of the bill of rights last year I made it clear it was not our intention to embark on any such study. I outlined at that time the difficulties, physical and otherwise, that such a study would raise. I said we did not consider it appropriate to embark on that sort of study, but that what we proposed was that we would be on the alert for anything that might bring to our attention a case of conflict, particularly, of course, anything emerging from a judgment of the courts. If any court judgment were to say "We consider this to be in conflict with the bill of rights", that of course would have our immediate attention in so far as the matter was one within federal jurisdiction. I also said that as various acts come up for revision from time to time or for scrutiny in any way, we would certainly look at them from the particular point of view of the bill of rights, but that we did not intend to undertake a general survey of all the statute law of Canada from that point of view.
I must disagree with my hon. friend when he says that nothing has been done to bring existing statutes into conformity with the bill of rights. I would remind him of a discussion we had in this chamber not long ago in connection with the Fisheries Act, when my colleague the Minister of Fisheries presented a revision of that act. We were careful to point out, as I think was our duty, that certain of its provisions had been opened for the express purpose of revising them in order to bring them into line with the bill of rights. Those were the provisions relating to seizure and confiscation.
In legislation very shortly to be introduced in the house my hon. friend will see a case of another act certain provisions of which, now that it is up for revision, have been revised to bring them into conformity with the bill of rights.

Before the minister leaves the subject of the bill of rights, may I be permitted to ask another question. My recollection is that the Prime Minister said, I think at this session, there would be amendments brought in to the War Measures Act. bill that has not yet reached this house but notice of which exists. Is it the government's intention to proceed with amendments to the War Measures Act during this session?

My department has been working on amendments to the War Measures Act. We are not at the moment in a position to recommend legislation. I therefore regret that I am unable to assure the hon. member that an amending measure will be proceeded with at this session.

However, whichever it was, my recollection is that reference was made to action being taken at this session.

If we should find ourselves in that position, and if there should be an immediate demand for action, we would then do our best to proceed; but I must say that in view of the stage the session has reached, and the state of the order paper, I think probably we all might wish to have another look at that situation.
The final question the hon. member raised concerned the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. The hon. member asked me what was the position with regard to new legislation in that field. I am very glad to be able to advise my hon. friend that if he will refer to my policy statement made on January 24 in this house on behalf of myself and my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare, he will see there a fairly complete outline of the policy which we have developed with respect to these matters, particularly with respect to those aspects which come under my responsibility, namely the custody and treatment of addicts. If my hon. friend will look at Votes and Proceedings of yesterday he will see there notice of a motion in the name of the Minister of National Health and Welfare in these words:
-On Monday next-Bill intituled: "An act to provide for the control of narcotic drugs".
That legislation will be introduced, if the house gives leave, on Monday. The bill is printed and will be available for distribution at first reading.
I am pleased to be able to say that we have developed what we believe to be a sound and forward looking policy-and I am glad to be able to have some part in this-after so many years during which the Canadian people have been hoping for a forward step in connection with the treatment of drug

addicts. We believe we have developed a sound policy. I do not wish to be too optimistic, because it is an extremely difficult field, but I can assure the committee that the legislation, when introduced, will, I believe, come up to the expectations of the Canadian people and their desire to see, after all these years, a real effort made to come to grips with the drug problem.
The hon. member for Skeena asked me what is the situation with regard to the Eccles divorce case. I find that in reporting to the committee two days ago as to how I am dealing with allegations of irregularities in those divorce cases that are referred to me, I omitted one stage in the process that we have worked out. I believe I said that when these cases are referred to me I make certain inquiries including, for instance, an inquiry from the chairman of the Senate divorce committee, and gather all the material that seems to be relevant, and then transmit it to the appropriate provincial attorney general. I omitted to state that one of the stages in this process is to refer the material to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for investigation so that the facts can be established. Then, when that is completed, all the documents including the R.C.M.P. report, are referred to the appropriate attorney general. The Eccles case is now under investigation but I have not made a report to the provincial attorney general, although we have had some preliminary correspondence with Toronto about this case.
In addition to the Eccles case there are three others which were referred to me and which are undergoing the same process, the Isenberg, Leduc and Godard cases. One other, the Radakovitz case, has been directed to my attention and I have referred it to Senator Roebuck for such information as he may be able to let me have from the records of the Senate committee. This case has not yet been referred to the police for investigation, but the other four have been referred.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether this action arises from the activities of the R.C.M.P. or from those of the attorney general himself, but it has been brought to my attention that the activities of the R.C.M.P. in the Eccles case have placed one of the parties to the case in an unfortunate position. I am informed that Mr. Eccles attempted to obtain a transcript of the evidence heard before the miscellaneous private bills committee last year when the case was reheard by that committee, but has been refused it because it is considered a private document. In his words that is what happened. If any two people should be entitled to obtain that transcript surely they

would be Mr. and Mrs. Eccles. The transcript should be made available to them.
I understand also that recently an R.C.M.P. officer of unknown rank whose name is Webster phoned Mr. Eccles in Toronto and requested an appointment the following day, to which request Mr. Eccles acceded. The following morning at 9:30 two R.C.M.P. officers visited Mr. Eccles and sought to obtain information which Mr. Eccles refused to give on the ground that he was alone and there were two officers present. Perhaps Mr. Eccles is sceptical about the police in this regard. The questions related to times and dates and other information given in evidence in the committee. The police officers indicated that they had read, reviewed and studied the transcript of evidence given before the committee.
Mr. Eccles was placed in an unfair position. Before any additional inquiries are made of any of the parties to or witnesses in the Eccles case, they should be given an opportunity to examine the transcript of evidence to refresh their memories, which may be hazy concerning some of the evidence given before that committee. I wonder whether somehow or other, perhaps through the minister in consultation with the R.C.M.P. or the attorney general, we could ensure that no further inquiries are made by the R.C.M.P. of individuals who have given evidence before the committee unless those individuals have had an opportunity to be in possession of the transcript of evidence.
I wish to point out one other thing here. On the morning the two R.C.M.P. officers went to see Mr. Eccles-when there were two of them and one of him, as it were-he was rather busy and asked if they could come back, which they did. In the meantime I understand Mr. Eccles got in touch with two other gentlemen-as witnesses, if anything, I suppose-who were reporters for the Toronto Star. When the two R.C.M.P. officers returned they found these two gentlemen there and refused to go any further into the inquiry or questioning they had originally intended to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

In answer to those questions, Mr. Chairman, first the conference of commissioners on uniformity of legislation in Canada meets once a year. It comprises representatives of the attorneys general of the provinces and the Attorney General of Canada. It always meets immediately prior to the annual meeting of the Canadian Bar Association. Its primary task is to consider all those suggestions that are from time to time brought forward with respect to amendments to the Criminal Code.
The reason for this conference, as will be appreciated, is that the criminal law is enforced through the medium of provincial attorneys general although it is enacted here in parliament. Therefore many years ago it was thought desirable to set up some regular machinery through which representatives of the provincial attorneys general could meet with representatives of the Attorney General of Canada to discuss the implications of various suggested amendments to the Criminal Code that are made from time to time. We make a small grant to that body.
Before the minister continues, Mr. Chairman, could we be informed of the reason for the contribution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am informed that every government contributes. I am told that other governments contribute the same amount. The purpose of the contribution is to meet the cost of printing, correspondence and stationery-printing reports and so on-because there is a good deal of work carried on by the secretary of the conference during the year while suggested amendments are accumulating. These all have to be processed and distributed. Then, as I said, the commissioners meet every year during the week prior to the Canadian Bar Association meeting and go through the material that has been prepared for their consideration.
The answer to the question with regard to grants to the recognized private after-care agencies is this. Until this year the grants were made from two sources, one the Department of Justice itself and the other the penitentiaries branch. When the parole board came into being two years ago, that portion

Supply-Justice
of the grant which had formerly been administered by the department was put under the parole board item. That is why last year there was an item, as is shown here, of $60,000.
This year, however, we decided there was not much point in haying two different items for grants to the same agencies, so we decided to consolidate them into one sum. We have placed it under the item for departmental administration. Last year the total provided was $150,000, of which $60,000 was paid by the parole board and $90,000 by the penitentiaries branch. This year there is an increase of $17,500 in the over-all amount, making a total of $167,500.

Mr. Chairman, I am interested in the Eccles case because it is the only case we have had of that nature which we have been able to follow. As reported on page 581 of Hansard for December 7, 1960, the hon. member for Skeena asked a question about the position of the Eccles case at that time. In answering that question the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice had this to say:
I am informed that the law officers of the crown, after a careful review of this case and all the facts as presented by the committee, have referred it to the department of the attorney general of Ontario for consideration as to possible action under the Criminal Code, particularly referring to perjury.
It has been referred to the provincial authorities because it is a matter concerning the administration of justice within a province.
My question is, how did the R.C.M.P. get back into this case? I realize that the minister, replying to another question addressed to him by myself on March 2, 1961, as reported at page 2575 of Hansard, said:
As the hon. member has pointed out, this matter was referred by us to the attorney general of Ontario, and since the initial reference certain further investigations into some aspects of the case are being conducted. The results of those investigations will in turn be brought to the attention of the department of the attorney general of Ontario. As my parliamentary secretary indicated to the house on December 7, 1960, this matter relates to the administration of justice in the province.
How did the R.C.M.P. get back into this case if the investigation was being conducted by the province of Ontario? I am told by Mr. Eccles that nobody has been to see him about this matter, apart from this investigation which took place very recently when, first of all, an R.C.M.P. plainclothes man identified himself as such and then wanted to discuss the case. Then followed the incident which the hon! member for Skeena has outlined. This would appear to indicate that either the minister has reopened the case himself, going

further than he indicated on March 2, or that the R.C.M.P. are acting on behalf of the Ontario attorney general.

As I explained a few moments ago in answer to the last inquiry from the hon. member for Skeena, there is a stage at which the R.C.M.P. conducts an investigation into the facts as alleged and as they appear from the documents. The R.C.M.P. report on their investigation is referred to the appropriate attorney general. I told the committee a few moments ago this was the procedure we had worked out. The Eccles case was the first of these which came to us, so we thought we had better work out a suitable procedure. Early this year we wrote to the attorney general of Ontario advising him we had received these complaints. Then, in accord with the answer I have already given, there were preliminary discussions with the attorney general of Ontario. Later my deputy went to Toronto to interview the officials of the attorney general's department there in order to work out a completely satisfactory procedure.
It was pointed out by the attorney general of Ontario or by officials of his department that it was felt they should have the responsibility for any prosecutions for perjury or other ordinary offences under the Criminal Code which might take place in Ontario. However, in this case, and it might well be in other cases, the offences were alleged to have taken place in more than one province. In that particular case some of the offences and irregularities alleged were said to have taken place in Quebec. So the attorney general of Ontario suggested that since the records were initially all available here, and since in many of these cases there was activity going on in more than one province, it might be appropriate for the R.C.M.P. to conduct the investigation into whatever it was alleged had been improper and then, when we had concluded that investigation, to convey the files, the police report and all the other documents to the Attorney General of Ontario who would look at them from the point of view of whether prosecution is called for. This was the arrangement worked out, and it is the arrangement being followed in this case.

168.	Exchequer Court of Canada-Administration, $151,110.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for straightening me out in regard to this item. I assume that the remarks I made before the luncheon recess, during our consideration of vote 167, will apply here, and that it will be unnecessary for me to repeat them.
At the present time there are courts with jurisdiction to handle divorce cases in each province of Canada with the exception of Quebec and Newfoundland. As is well known, divorces from these provinces are brought to the House of Commons, handled by a committee of the other place, and then finally granted by an act of this parliament. The handling of divorces from those two provinces in this way was the subject of considerable discussion in this house last session. Undoubtedly the same sort of discussion will take place this session if the divorce bills presently before parliament are proceeded with. In any event, I feel sure that each member of this house, as well as each member of that other place and, of course, a considerable portion of the general public of Canada, feels that the present system in this regard is a cumbersome and inefficient one, and that

Supply-Justice
parliament should not be the arena or court dealing with these particular matters.
I realize, ol course, there is some objection in the province of Quebec to the setting up of courts with jurisdiction to handle divorce cases from that province. I am not aware that a similarly strong objection is taken to this procedure in the province of Newfoundland, perhaps because there are relatively few divorce cases arising in that province.
There have been alternative methods of proceeding with divorce cases from those two provinces suggested from time to time. Without going into detail in respect of those alternatives, I wish to deal with the jurisdiction of the exchequer court in this regard.
The suggestion that the exchequer court deal with divorce cases from those provinces is perhaps not completely acceptable as an alternative providing a complete solution to the problem. However, should the jurisdiction of the exchequer court be enlarged to cover divorce cases from Quebec and Newfoundland, I suggest they would be more expeditiously dealt with than they presently are, under the petition and private bill system, and perhaps at a lower cost. I also suggest that under this alternative system there should be a more careful consideration and review of the evidence presented in support of the individual divorce cases than is received under the present system.
While this alternative method is perhaps not completely acceptable, I feel the government should take cognizance of that suggestion, with a view to making a decision in respect of amending the Exchequer Court Act, increasing that court's jurisdiction to cover petitions for divorce originating in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland. Even though this sort of approach would perhaps deal only with divorces on the grounds which exist at the present time, it would not be wise to extend the grounds as well as the jurisdiction at this time. This is a finality we must look toward. I do not think that further legislative action should be taken unilaterally by the federal government but only after consultation with the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland because certainly they have an interest in this particular matter. It may well be that after consultation with these two provinces it might be decided that this sort of action would be an acceptable alternative to that which exists at the moment. Perhaps it might be found desirable to have the cases heard by the exchequer court in the city of Ottawa if another course is found to be objectionable by the province of Quebec itself.

I say that the granting of such jurisdiction to the exchequer court would bring about a more expeditious dispatch of the cases because when one proceeds by way of a petition to parliament one must comply with the rules of the Senate in so far as petitions are concerned. There is a time limit within which those petitions may be presented. It is only during the early days after the opening of the session that such petitions can be accepted. It is only by consent that petitions which are presented later are accepted by the Senate and by the house. The system used at present prohibits an individual from proceeding with a divorce action when parliament is not in session. During recesses of parliament and in the time between the dissolution and the calling of a new parliament the present system prohibits people in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland from taking action for divorce. Then, the time limit established by the rules of this house and by the Senate with respect to the presentation of petitions confines this period to a relatively few days during the year.
For argument's sake, if one of the parties to a marriage discovered that his or her spouse had committed adultery in any province other than Quebec or Newfoundland action would be instituted in the courts almost immediately and, depending on the business before the court, the case could be heard within a relatively short period of time, and the court would come to a decision. If the same set of circumstances were to occur in Quebec or Newfoundland it would mean that the aggrieved party would have to wait until the opening of the next session of parliament, whenever that might be, before a petition could be presented and the machinery set in motion to deal with the particular case.
At the moment, under the present system of petitioning parliament for divorce-and this has been authenticated by lawyers who have been active in these particular cases and by petitioners and respondents as well -the costs amount to a minimum of some $1,500. This is for the open and shut case, without any extensive work being performed by private detectives and without any contestation on the part of the respondent, or the corespondent, that adultery did not take place. If there is protestation, if a case requires extensive, or any degree of investigation on the part of a private detective or detectives, the fees and costs range upwards from $1,500. I have heard figures cited ranging from $10,000 to $15,000 as the total cost

to the petitioner in obtaining evidence, providing witnesses, paying private bill fees, lawyers' fees and the like, in order to get the case before parliament.
I have heard figures cited by lawyers in other provinces with respect to an open and shut case, as they are referred to in provincial courts, and they run somewhere in the neighbourhood of $400 to $500. If we compare $400 to $500 with a minimum of $1,500 as the cost for parliamentary divorces we shall see that our present system is imposing a pretty heavy burden upon residents in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland when it comes to divorce actions. The saying has been bruited about to some extent that this system allows divorces for the rich and just misery and continued misery for the poor.
If the exchequer court were given this jurisdiction it would not be the complete answer to what exists at the moment because I doubt very much whether we could give to the exchequer court any jurisdiction in the field of alimony payments or any jurisdiction over the custody or welfare of children, since this is a matter which comes within provincial jurisdiction. Nevertheless, if we were to give this sort of jurisdiction to the Exchequer Court of Canada to deal with divorce actions arising in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland on the grounds that exist at the present time in the other provinces except Nova Scotia, where cruelty is also a ground for divorce, I think we would alleviate a great deal of the suffering, misery, and financial burdens which rest upon the shoulders of people in Quebec and Newfoundland who feel aggrieved and wish to take action for divorce. It would help somewhat in this regard and it would certainly remove from parliament what I consider to be a debasing task, namely the handling of divorce actions arising in those two provinces.
On a previous occasion the minister made some comments as to what might be done in this regard and I should certainly like to have his comments as to what studies have been made by his department and by the government with respect to this particular situation which has been advanced before in this parliament and in previous parliaments by members who are not here now. I know it is something that previous governments have considered. I think it would be well if the minister could indicate to the committee what progress is being made, if any, and what steps are being taken, if any, to deal with the divorce problem and specifically to deal with the suggestion which I have just made and which has been advanced in another form on other occasions by my friend from Timiskaming.

Quite apart from the consideration of whether there is a constitutional or jurisdictional obstacle in the way of transferring jurisdiction to the exchequer court, such a course would involve the enactment of a divorce law, and the parliament of Canada would then be in the position of having to enact a divorce law for a province. My hon. friend can readily appreciate just what sort of problems that would create.
