I do not think I really need to go much further. That sums up the whole of the problem. So far as the particular proposal is concerned, that is, the transferring of jurisdiction to the exchequer court, there are methods by which parliament itself may alter its own routine in the handling of these petitions for private bills dissolving marriage, but that is a matter for parliament to determine. Some hon. members have given study to this matter and, as is known, a private member introduced a bill in this chamber. The disposition of that bill is within the knowledge of the hon. member. It seems to me this does establish that parliament itself has the power to make what alterations it wishes in the method by which it deals with this matter, but there would have to be agreement, of course, upon the course to be followed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Has the minister considered the simple expedient of changing the one clause with respect to domicile and making provision in matters of divorce for Canadian domicile only rather than provincial domicile as at present? If provision were made for Canadian domicile in matters of divorce, would that not eliminate the problem that the minister has raised? The dominion of Canada divorce act of 1930 would then apply if that one change were made with respect to domicile. The only problem that would then face the government would be to make the necessary minor changes to provide for the addition of one or two judges to the exchequer court to deal with this specific matter solely. These judges would not travel but would sit here in the city of Ottawa to hear divorce petitions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With respect, I do not think that the matter is quite as straightforward as has been suggested in the remarks just made. My understanding is that the act of 1930 is not a substantive law of divorce. It deals primarily with the right of a wife to petition notwithstanding that her husband is not domiciled in one of the provinces of Canada. It seems to me that the implication of what is being suggested, however it was carried out, is that we would then have in the exchequer court an alternative court of divorce for all of Canada. There is no substantive law of divorce enacted by way of a federal statute. The law on this matter is the law that happens to be applicable in the various provinces by virtue of the sources, mainly in the United Kingdom, that were applicable at the time when the province entered confederation. So you actually have different laws of divorce applicable to the different provinces of Canada and, as I understand the legal situation, there is no single federal substantive divorce law in effect.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It is true that in the case of provinces like Nova Scotia, British Columbia, I believe, and one or two others, there was a law respecting divorce in their constitution at the time of confederation. Is it not true, however, that the Dominion of Canada did pass a law and that law is the only one that can be made applicable by any province that did not have such a provision at the time of confederation? The 1930 act is in effect the only law that can be made applicable in such a province. All we are suggesting is that the exchequer court is an alternative for those provinces that do not wish to do this.
I am suggesting that the only change that would be necessary would be to alter the requirement respecting domicile that is now in the act. As the situation is now, the domicile is that of the husband unless the wife has been deserted by the husband for a certain period of time. In that case the domicile of the wife applies. It seems to me that the act of 1930 applies to those provinces that have entered confederation since 1867. If, for example, the Northwest Territories becomes a province, the only act that can apply is the dominion act as it exists now and which is now being applied to that territory. We suggest that if provision were made for Canadian domicile in matters of divorce only it would be possible to bring a divorce action in many provinces and in those in which it was not possible such actions could be brought before the federal court. I would think that legally the government already has this right if they wish to apply it. I do not want to belabour the point but it seems to me that this is a very easy way of solving the problem.
I should like to refer in passing to what the minister said about the private member's bill that we passed. I believe this action was taken by all members of the house in their desire to find a solution to the problem but the other place has not seen fit to endorse the action. The minister will recall that the bill only applies to this year in any event. I think it has been the desire of the house that this problem be solved and that this solution should not be considered to be permanent, but only temporary in order to eliminate what many of us think is a moral problem. I refer to ruling upon situations about which we are not aware and about which we are not in a position to do anything. I am not a lawyer and I do not know all the legal implications, but from a study of this matter I would think it warrants new and immediate consideration because this suggestion would seem to me to be a solution of the problem.
I should like to add this. The provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland are in the position where they do not want to or are not able,

for various reasons, to establish courts of their own in this field. It seems to me that the objection which citizens of those provinces have should be removed and they should have the opportunity of bringing their cases to a federal court, if that is the only way open to them.
I think this objection will be met as long as we do not ask the province of Quebec, for example, to have exchequer court judges hearing these cases in that province. I think this would be the least offensive method of handling what is considered to be, and probably rightly so, a major social problem in that province. I do not want to belabour this question, but I think the minister would be well advised to give consideration to this matter because I see less objection to this method than to any other which I have examined, and I have examined seven or eight methods that could be used to solve this problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member may well have a point there and we will be glad to give further consideration to it. However, I think I am right in saying that if there is to be jurisdiction established in the exchequer court, to make it effective we would have to enact a substantive law of divorce applicable to the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland. It might be done with reference to the old English matrimonial causes act, which happens to be in force in British Columbia, but it would have to be an act of this parliament which brought into force a substantive law of divorce for those provinces.
I need only refer to that fact for my hon. friends to see the extent to which it bristles with problems. I am sure we are all interested in finding some solution that will be satisfactory to all concerned and we will be glad to give further consideration to the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Skeena.

Mr. Chairman, I had initially understood the minister's remarks to be a delightful way of saying no, but I see he has revised that somewhat and the suggestion is now going to be considered. I do not know whether the minister has the same sort of file as his colleague, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources-I think his colleague calls it an active consideration file -but I think this is something that should be put into that file for consideration.
I should like to deal with the minister's point that parliament, by following this course, would be enacting a substantive law of divorce for two provinces. If we followed the course advanced, that of giving jurisdiction to the exchequer court for these two
Supply-Justice
provinces, I think this is what we would be doing. But this course is not unprecedented in Canada.
The four western provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan have some pre-confederation, United Kingdom law that is applicable. This has something to do with the original jurisdiction of those courts. As anyone who has read about this will recall, at one time in the 1920's and before, people resident in Ontario used to petition parliament for divorce in the same manner as do residents of Quebec and Newfoundland. In the 1920's-1927, 1928 or in that general period-the founder of the C.C.F., the late J. S. Woodsworth, raised this question of divorce in parliament on grounds somewhat similar to those advanced last session by the hon. member for Timis-kaming, myself and other hon. members.
As a result of that the parliament of Canada -I think this was some time in the late 1920's -enacted a substantive law for the province of Ontario. That substantive law was the law of the United Kingdom as of a particular date. I forget the date; I think it was somewhere around 1857, but I am not certain about that. In any event, the parliament of Canada took action some 30 years ago to enact a substantive law of divorce for one of the provinces of Canada, namely Ontario.
There were difficulties to overcome at that time in connection with the relationship of the province of Ontario to the federal government. I do not know how the government of Canada and the government of Ontario reached agreement on this question or whether they even discussed the possibility of reaching agreement, but certainly it is not beyond the realm of possibility that parliament, having enacted a substantive law of divorce for a province in the past, can do so again. I do not think this raises any insurmountable problem with regard to taking a similar course of action in connection with two other provinces of Canada.
I think it does require, in addition to study or consideration by the minister and the government, perhaps direct consultation in a private way, if that is desirable, with the attorneys general or the governments of the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland to see whether or not some mutually agreeable arrangement could be worked out that would be acceptable to the residents and the governments of those provinces and the government of Canada. I suggest this course be followed by the minister.
I presume that the minister is in contact with the Attorney General of the province of Quebec about other matters concerned with divorce, namely allegations of perjury, collusion, condonation or the like. Surely it

Supply-Justice
would not be beyond the bounds of reason to ask that some preliminary, if only preliminary, discussions take place-if they have not taken place already-with the governments of these two provinces to see whether or not some mutual agreement can be reached on this matter.
I think that parliament, having enacted a substantive law of divorce for the province of Ontario some 30 years ago could do so again. No great difficulties have arisen since that time, and no constitutional problem arose then. Apparently it was perfectly constitutional for the parliament of Canada to do this in the 1920's, and it would appear to be perfectly constitutional to do it in 1961, 1962 or some time in the 1960's with respect to the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland.

Mr. Chairman, one thing that has always struck me as I read the estimates of the Department of Justice from year to year has been the salary provided for the registrars of the two most important courts in this country, namely the exchequer court and the Supreme Court of Canada. I note that the salary of the registrar in this item is $9,000 which is less than that which is paid to a junior counsel in the justice department. The justice department have a number of counsel who are paid from $17,500 or more, downwards. Here is a man who has a rank I think of a deputy minister and who is handling very important duties in one of our highest courts in the land, who is taxing bills running into tens of thousands of dollars, travelling between or from Victoria to St. John's, Newfoundland handling both admiralty cases and other cases coming under federal jurisdiction. Whatever has happened-and this is not the fault of this administration only-in the justice department over so many years cannot be understood, namely why the registrars of the Supreme Court of Canada should be paid only $11,500 when the counsel of the justice department are paid up to $17,500 or $20,000, and why the registrar of the exchequer court should receive less than the amount received by the registrar of the supreme court in local jurisdictions in the province of Ontario.
I should like to have the opinion of the Minister of Justice on this matter. I would rather be assured by him that something is going to be done. As a matter of fact if he will look back at the salary provided for this year in the previous item for the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada he will find that it is shown at $11,500 and that of the deputy registrar at only $10,500. As far as the registrar of the Exchequer Court of Canada is concerned, his salary is $9,000,

but the range of deputy registrar runs up to $9,800. I feel that the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada should receive the salary of a junior deputy minister in the government and certainly the same comment applies with respect to the registrar of the Exchequer Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not too happy about the salary levels in the courts, I must say. However, my hon. friend knows that it is not always the easiest thing in the world to get salaries revised. There has been some change in the position to which he last referred. I am trying to see if I can get the details in this regard from my officials. There has been a change, I believe, since the book was printed. The information I have now as to the registrar of the Exchequer Court of Canada is that his salary is authorized at $11,000. It is true that the deputy registrar's salary still ranges between $8,120 and $9,800. For the Supreme Court of Canada the registrar's salary is $13,000. Therefore, it will be seen that there have been increases of $2,000 in each case.
While that is something a little bit better I think the minister will agree with me that owing to the fact-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt in order to correct myself. In the case of the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada the increase was $1,500, from $11,500 to $13,000.

The minister realizes that this is his department and that this matter is not subject to the civil service commission. As a man of law and one who has had contact with the courts, I think he realizes that having regard to the duties of these two officials, these increases are hardly in keeping with the dignity of the office which these men occupy.

This item includes not only exchequer court judges salaries and, I take it, also their travelling expenses or travelling allowances, but also includes the salaries of district judges in admiralty and their travelling allowances. Can the minister give us an indication, just to show the extent of the work of these two judicial divisions, what the travelling allowances of the district judges in admiralty are and what has been the travelling allowances of the judges of the exchequer court?

The salaries of the district judges in admiralty are as follows: Four at $1,000; one at $800; one at $600; three at $333.33. With regard to their travelling allowances may I say this. The travelling allowance of the president and the puisne

judges of the exchequer court are included this year in the estimates at $7,500. The last figure I have-that is the actual expenses for 1959-60-is $7,649. The travelling allowance for the admiralty judges is $500. The actual expenditures in 1959-60 was $148.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
169. Administration of justice in the Northwest Territories including the Northwest Territories territorial court, $154,794.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On this vote, I am interested in obtaining some information. I notice that on the order paper today we have a resolution in the name of the minister. Its purpose is to provide for two additional puisne judges of the superior court of Quebec and one additional judge for the court of appeal of British Columbia. I should like to ask the minister this question. Are these judges allowed to take work outside of their own field, particularly in matters pertaining to provincial jurisdiction, and are they allowed to receive remuneration for so doing? The reason I ask these questions is that I have heard a number of complaints about superior court judges who, on being asked to sit on such and such a case, have said, "no, I am not available". They have said they were writing something in connection with arbitration,-
A conciliation report.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: -a report on either arbitration cases or conciliation cases for boards on which they sat. There are numbers, I understand, who normally would be available to travel from one part to another to fill in and take cases not directly in their own area but they are unable to do this in many instances. They say, "I cannot go today because I have an arbitration board report to write", or "I have a conciliation board report to write" or "I am sitting on such and such a board". We are not referring to those judges who come to the minister and ask him for permission to undertake a certain job for the provincial government, such as the two judges in Quebec who, I understand, have asked for and received permission to make an inquiry into the whole judicial set-up in that province. That is not what we are referring to. We refer to the other jobs that superior court judges are doing. The questions I wish to ask are these. Do they have the right to do this? Do they have to get permission from the minister? Are they allowed to receive remuneration while they are doing work in a provincial jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to whether judges can sit outside the territorial limits of the province in which they are appointed, the answer is 90205-6-346
Supply-Justice
yes with regard to the judges of the court of appeal of British Columbia. By an amendment last year we provided for a change in the constitution of the appeal court in the Yukon territory. Formerly, it had been the appeal court of British Columbia and an appellant from the Yukon had to go down to Vancouver or Victoria to have his appeal heard. Last year we changed that, so it is possible now to constitute a court of appeal and have it sit in the Yukon territory. A judge of the court of appeal of British Columbia may go up and sit with other judges designated to constitute that court of appeal. He would receive no extra remuneration for that work but would, of course, be entitled to his travelling expenses. This is one of the reasons why provision is made for the salary of an extra judge of the court of appeal of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I take it the arrangement which the minister has described has proved to be a satisfactory one. Has any consideration been given to making a similar arrangement in the northern areas of Alberta, Saskatchewan and, possibly, Manitoba to extend the scope of the court of appeal so that it might hear whatever appeals arise in the Northwest Territories?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My recollection is that we did the same thing with respect to the Northwest Territories last year by the use of the court of appeal of Alberta, Yellowknife being the administrative capital as it were. That is not strictly accurate, but it is the main centre and it is the place where the judge of the Northwest Territories presides. It is most conveniently reached from Edmonton. That is why we avail ourselves of the services of a judge from the court of appeal of Alberta in connection with appeals in the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister said something about superior court judges within provinces who were taking extra work in arbitration and conciliation proceedings. The charge is being made that the reason why cases are piling up in the superior courts is because some of these judges are taking work outside their jurisdiction. Such a practice is said to have given rise to delays in judicial proceedings, and I should like to ask the minister whether he is consulted and whether his permission is obtained before extra work of this kind is undertaken. I should further like to ask whether the law as it now stands allows superior court judges to accept remuneration for work done outside their jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Judges Act provides in effect that if authorized by the lieutenant

Supply-Justice
governor in council a judge of a superior court may act as a commissioner or arbitrator on any commission of inquiry or arbitration to which he may be appointed by any authority exercisable in that behalf by the lieutenant governor in council, so the act does provide authority for judges to act as commissioners or arbitrators. The act also states clearly that no judge so acting shall receive any extra remuneration. This is, then, in effect, made part of his judicial duties and a judge is not to receive extra pay in respect of such extra duties, though he is entitled to transportation expenses and living allowances which may be required in the course of his duty as commissioner or arbitrator.

Perhaps I could pursue this question a little further. I understand the minister to be referring now to duties such as those of an arbitrator appointed, say, pursuant to a provincial arbitration act where decisions involving property and land have to be reached with respect to valuation. The question raised by my hon. friend from Tim-iskaming concerns the work of judges as chairman of arbitration boards and conciliation boards in labour matters. I wonder how this aspect of judicial duties is governed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member would have to consult the statutes that are applicable. The words used in the Judges Act are these:
-may act as commissioner or arbitrator on any commission, inquiry or arbitration for which he may be appointed under any authority in that behalf exercisable by the governor in council or the lieutenant governor in council respectively.
So if the provincial statute authorized the appointment by order in council of a judge to act as chairman of an arbitration board, or as a member of that board, it would come within the provisions of the Judges Act.

But suppose the appointment was made by a cabinet minister? For instance, as I recall the labour relations act of the province of British Columbia it is the minister of labour who appoints the chairman of the conciliation board, not the lieutenant governor in council. I assume that in such a case the provisions of the act would not apply.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is some danger in my making precise answers on general questions, but I would say, generally speaking that in such cases the consent of the governor in council here would have to be obtained. If it involves an appointment other than one that the lieutenant governor in council might be authorized to make, then the judge should obtain consent here.

This question was discussed, the minister will recall, in the first session after 1957. I have not referred to Hansard to verify whether or not my memory is correct, but I believe the minister said at that time that he proposed to look into the question I then raised. My question arose out of a direction given by the chief justice of the trial division in the province of Ontario that those judges who served under his immediate direction should confine themselves exclusively to their judicial duties. There was concern about their participation in the work of boards of all kinds, arbitration boards, conciliation boards and other kinds of quasi-judicial bodies. I was prompted at the time to ask the minister what his view was with regard to such judges who came under his jurisdiction, judges of the Supreme Court of Canada particularly. I do not know whether this would apply with any force at all to judges of the exchequer court. I asked this question in order to ascertain what the view of the minister was.
Since that time the hon. gentleman has had an opportunity to acquire considerably more experience in his administrative duties and he may be in a position to tell the committee today what he thinks about this problem. On one hand we have the labour unions who have very strong views, I take it, against the use of judges on conciliation boards and the like. There are others interested in the administration of justice, members of the legal profession and others, who believe that the judicial function is one which as far as possible should be confined to its own particular field. Has the minister any views which he would care to express to the committee at this time?
I know the minister says that under the Judges Act a judge may act with respect to any matter which arises out of a direction given by the lieutenant governor in council but as the hon. member for Skeena has pointed out there are certain types of conciliation boards in labour disputes which afford to the minister in charge of the department and, in some cases, to the deputy minister, authority to designate an individual or individuals as a member or members of a conciliation board. We are developing in Canada, as they are in the United States and as they are, of course, in Great Britain -I suppose it is general in all modern industrial societies-a set of circumstances which requires the use of judicial experience and the judicial temperament outside the actual determination of matters which are directly related to the interpretation of the law in civil or criminal cases. There are many instances where, I am sure, the judicial

technique exercised by a properly appointed judicial person could make a much more useful contribution than people who are not trained in the sifting of evidence, and in the process of adjudication which lend themselves to more reliable determinations. I should be interested to know what the minister feels in this regard.
I realize in regard to the use of judges of the Supreme Court of Canada there is a divided view; a view, I take it, which is divided in that court itself. Different ministers of justice have taken different views with regard to the use of judges of the final court of appeal in respect of matters involving labour disputes, royal commissions and the like. I am not at this moment quarreling with their participation, but seeking to ascertain the view of the minister in regard to this matter. It becomes a matter of increasing importance in respect of the Supreme Court of Canada because, since the abolition of appeals to the judicial committee, that court has taken on an authority and, in consequence, a juridical prestige, which I am sure we are all pleased to see, and hope will grow.
Judges of the United States supreme court do not, I believe, take part in extrajudicial activities, with perhaps the exception of the chief justice, and their work is confined essentially to the work on the bench. I believe I am right in saying that in the United Kingdom it has not been the practice that those who sit on the judicial committee take part in commissions and the like. Excuse me, I am wrong in saying that. In the case of members of the judicial committee there are well known individuals, such as Lord MacMillan, who have taken part in royal commissions and the like. However, in the United Kingdom, I believe it has not been the practice for those judges who sit on the final court of appeal, as it were, in respect of domestic matters, to serve in a non-judicial capacity: I should like to know what the situation is here in this regard, and I address my remarks particularly in respect of the Supreme Court of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a word or two before the Minister of Justice speaks. I think the point raised by the hon. member for Essex East is of very great importance, and I should like the minister to recall that a former highly respected member of this house, known to both the minister and the hon. member for Essex East, the late John Hackett, had very strong reservations in respect of judges being appointed special duties because he feared, if they were drawn into matters which were controversial, particularly election petitions 90205-6-346J
Supply-Justice
and things of that kind, the absolute impartiality which is so essential to the performance of their duties on the bench might be impaired by this extrajudicial function. I mention that fact because I know it will be of interest to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this stage I do not wish to go beyond what I said on earlier occasions, to which my friend the hon. member for Essex East has referred. I do not in any sense retract anything I said at that time, but at the moment I do not wish to go beyond that. At that time I gave a fairly extensive outline of my views regarding this question.
I can re-emphasize, however, my view that it is one thing for a judge to be asked to sit in a quasi-judicial capacity, as chairman of an arbitration board, where he is exercising at least a quasi-judicial function in the arbitration of issues, but it is a very different thing for a judge to act as chairman of a conciliation board, where he is mediating between parties, which seems to me to be foreign to judicial functions. That is almost inevitably bound to make him, in the eyes of one or other of the parties, a partisan, when the results are given. The results will favour one or other of the parties, because the judge has been carrying on mediation. It seems to me that a clear distinction can be drawn in this area and, as I said earlier, in saying so, I am not making any firm pronouncement regarding the use of judges in respect of arbitration boards. I think this practice should be resorted to rarely so as not to become the custom, because judges should spend the vast majority of their time in performing their essential judicial functions on the bench.
I should also perhaps give some indication of the attitude of this government toward the matter, certainly so far as the supreme and exchequer courts of Canada are concerned. Evidence of this attitude is found in the fact that since we assumed office in June of 1957, we have not appointed any judge from either of these courts to any outside board, commission or inquiry. That is a record which I hope we will be able to maintain.

Mr. Chairman, the minister quoted earlier from a statute concerning what a superior court judge may do in respect of duties outside his court functions, if that judge is appointed by the lieutenant governor in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Those provisions are to be found in sections 37 and 38 of the Judges Act. Perhaps I should make quite clear what I have said. I make no prohibition against the appointment of judges to the functions which

Supply-Justice
are described there. There may be cases where that is proper, and where, indeed, the only person acceptable under certain circumstances is a person holding high judicial office, and I do not want anyone to interpret me as saying that this must never and will never happen. I should like to be interpreted as saying that it is my view that this should happen as seldom as possible, if ever, and so far we have been able to live within those guiding lines.
I have referred the hon. member to sections 37 and 38 of the Judges Act. I should remind him that judges of superior courts in the provinces are judges of provincial courts. It is true they are appointed and paid by the federal government, and there are very good judicial reasons for that, but once they are appointed, they are judges of provincial courts. We would not be well founded in taking the position that the provinces cannot, by appropriate legislation, decide what will be the duties of those provincial judges, making those duties part of their judicial functions. However, the scheme of the act, as it presently is, reflects the importance of maintaining the position that this should not be a casual thing, but must be something for which legislative authority exists in the province, and the particular exercise of that authority, in so far as making appointments is concerned, is vested in the lieutenant governor in council.
I gather that if it is not within the authority of the lieutenant governor in council, but is a ministerial authority, then it is subject to the governor in council?
That is correct.
Perhaps the minister could indicate how often the governor in council has granted consent in comparison with the number of requests for consent which have been received during the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Requests which are received are comparatively few; I should suggest in the neighbourhood of three or four per year. I do not give that figure as a firm one, but I am sure I should realize if there were more than three or four. I do not think there are more requests than that received per year.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to-

Perhaps I may be allowed to follow this subject to its conclusion. I take it this procedure applies also in respect of appointments of chairmen to boards dealing with things such as labour disputes, in that

the consent of the governor in council must be acquired if a ministerial appointment is involved?
I certainly hope that is the case because, as I interpret the act, requests should be made here.

When a judge is appointed as a chairman of a conciliation or arbitration board under ministerial authority with the consent of the two parties to the dispute, and with the consent of the governor in council, what is the position in respect of remuneration for his services?

That is covered by the next section of the Judges Act, section 39, which says:
No judge shall receive any remuneration in addition to his judicial salary for acting as commissioner or arbitrator-*
And so on. Then, it is made subject to the provisions of subsection 3 which says he may receive travelling and living expenses which he ordinarily incurs while carrying on his duties as commissioner or arbitrator.
He may receive fees as chairman of a conciliation board? That is not prohibited?

I think this section is clear. It reads as follows:
(1) Except as provided in subsection (3), no judge shall receive any remuneration in addition to his judicial salary for acting as commissioner or arbitrator-
Then there are some other words which do not make the situation any clearer. Then we come to subsection 2 which reads:
Subsection (1) does not affect the right of any judge to receive remuneration under the provisions of any dominion or provincial statute in force on the 1st day of July, 1920.
Do not ask what the historical background of that is. I continue:
(3) A judge acting as commissioner or arbitrator pursuant to subsection (2) of section 38, or as administrator or deputy of the Governor General or performing any duty or service he is required to perform for or on behalf of the government of Canada or the government of any province, may receive, in addition to his judicial salary, such moving or transportation expenses and living allowance as the governor in council or the lieutenant governor in council, as the case may be, may fix by general or special order.

Mr. Chairman, some remarks were made a few minutes ago concerning the dignity of the bench. It seems to me it does not add dignity to the bench nor to our legal profession to have retired judges returning to practice before the bar and the courts where for many years they sat as presiding judges. I think this criticism is especially valid, as the hon. member for Essex East would agree, in matters in the

Supreme Court of Canada which, of course, is now the highest court in the land. One would hope that those retired judges are not forced to take this course of action because of economic necessity owing to the inadequacy of their pensions.
As a footnote to the same comment, Mr. Chairman, it has been noted and brought to my attention that in Ontario at least certain judges have used the title of their former position in furtherance of their own professional interests when they have returned to practice.

The practice of judges retiring from the courts, of course, is not one of recent origin. As a member of the bar, I can very well understand the concern of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken with regard to this matter. I rose not so much to pursue this aspect of the problem, although I am aware of its existence and its importance, as to ask what is the position, for instance, with regard to a county court judge-I do not want to identify the person because I have no reason to suspect his good intentions, nor do I in any way wish to reflect on the integrity of the person -who takes over the chairmanship, for instance, and the administration of the liquor control commission in one of our large provinces? I do not know whether the minister knows to whom my remarks are directed, but I wish to know whether that person has the right to continue to be regarded as a judge? What is -his status? Is he still a county court judge? I know this situation does not apply to the present chairman of the civil service commission who, on taking over that office, abandoned the right to the privileges that flows from the appointment as one of Her Majesty's judges in the supreme court of Ontario. I do not know whether that applies to his title. I think he bears the appellation "Mr." and not "hon. Mr. Justice". What I rose particularly to ask was this. What is the situation with regard to the particular assignment given to the individual who was a good county court judge and who I am sure is a man of great integrity, who continues to be regarded as a judge and continues to be called a judge, but who is administering an important position in a government department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The situation in that regard is not altogether clear, Mr. Chairman, and is one to which I hope to be in a position to bring some clarity at a time when I am able to present some general provisions revising the Judges Act in this regard. I cannot really say much more. If the hon. gentleman is really interested in following it up I might, with the greatest of good will, suggest that
Supply-Justice
possibly the answer to the situation is within his knowledge or his ability to obtain because it arose during the period of time when the government of which he was a member was holding office.

I do not want the matter to be left on that basis because I think on reflection the minister will regard that as not the way to leave it. It is true that the particular individual was appointed to this provincial post at a time when I happened to be in the government. The individual was appointed to this provincial post by a provincial government, and that appointment had nothing to do, of course, with his appointment as a judge, nominated for that purpose by a minister of justice serving the crown in the right of the federal government.
There is no law, of course, to prevent a judge duly appointed from taking an appointment of that kind. The minister may have some legislation in mind because he speaks about clarifying the situation sometime in the near future. It may be that the way to do it is by legislation, but it does seem to me that when we are so justifiably proud of our judicial system and of those who serve on the bench, whether in county court, district court or in superior court positions, we should be jealous about any act that in any way detracts from the dignity, the prestige and the authority of those courts and of those who sit in those courts. Of course the federal government cannot say to a provincial government, "You shall refrain from appointing a judge appointed by us to act in a purely administrative capacity". In the absence of legislative authority for that kind of direction the federal government cannot say that. It may be, as I said, that it will be necessary to provide that kind of enactment. The minister meets with attorneys general frequently, not only at constitutional conferences but on other occasions. It seems to me an effective way to deal with this situation is to have it clearly understood that judges are not to be used by federal or provincial executive bodies for that kind of purpose.
I am not now talking about sitting on commissions or boards. When I made my comment a few moments ago I did not express a view as to the merits. I was simply putting forward a statement for the purpose of ascertaining the minister's thinking in the matter. But appointing a judge to something that is not only extrajudicial but is entirely nonjudicial and nothing more than an administrative function is an altogether different matter, and I think it is a wrong use of experienced judicial personnel. I am not asking the minister to take steps now to cause something that has happened to be corrected.

Supply-Justice
However, I think it is only by a discussion of this kind that we can ascertain what is in the mind of the minister, and the discussion will serve to help him in the formulation of policy for the future.
I have no doubt that these things were done during the time that another government was in office, and I am not raising the matter in a critical way. The minister has said that during the time the present government has been in power and he has been Minister of Justice no judge of the Supreme Court of Canada has been used in any way that would place that judge in a position where he would be competing in a non-judicial function with some other person serving, let us say, on a board of arbitration. I think the minister is to be commended for that. I think that our supreme court judges in particular ought not to be used except in judicial functions so that they cannot be placed in a position where they are open to any kind of suggestion that has anything other than a judicial aspect to it. I raised the particular matter not because I expect the minister to correct the situation. He has said enough to satisfy me with regard to that situation, and it may be that this discussion will serve to encourage him to raise the matter when he discusses these questions further with the attorneys general.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I appreciate very much indeed what the hon. member has said. I think he and I share the same approach to this problem.
Before we carry this item, would the minister explain what is the substantive law of divorce that applies in the Northwest Territories and also the Yukon?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the statute that set up the Northwest Territories in 1870, I believe, the effect was that the matrimonial causes act then in force in the United Kingdom was made applicable in the Northwest Territories.
Did I understand the minister to say that this was contained in a statute establishing the Northwest Territories?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
It says in the statute that the law of divorce will be that of the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In effect, the laws of England as in force at the 1st of July, 1870, shall apply in the Northwest Territories to the extent they are applicable and are not excluded by special provisions of the laws of Canada. Similarly, when British Columbia entered confederation the same general situation was brought about. There was a provision in a
CMr. Martin (Essex East) .1
statute at the time of entry into confederation which had the effect of making applicable in British Columbia the laws of England as they were in force at certain dates.
Did I understand the minister to say that it was the statute which provided that British Columbia would have certain divorce laws? I understood it to be a court case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I had not intended to say that the statute made specific reference to divorce. The statute said that the laws of England in effect shall apply and, as a matter of fact, it took a couple of cases in the privy council to determine precisely what laws of England with respect to divorce and matrimonial causes were in effect then and were therefore applicable in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: How many divorce cases have there been in the Northwest Territories in the past year and where were they heard?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not have any figures on that because these are civil proceedings and therefore they do not come to my attention nor do I have any responsibility for them. I assume they would be heard in Yellowknife which is the judicial centre of the Northwest Territories and the place where Mr. Justice Sissons presides. Mr. Justice Sissons does go on circuit and I suppose he could hear a divorce case in a place other than Yellowknife but I do not know that he ever has. Yellowknife would be the normal place where these cases would be tried.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Combines Investigation Act-
171. Restrictive trade practices commission, $94,840.

Mr. Chairman, I think the practice followed last year and the year before, if not in other years, was that we dealt with the combines investigation branch and the restrictive practices commission under the same item, and I should like to follow somewhat the same approach. Under the activities of the branch I should like to raise again a specific and important matter relating to what is loosely referred to as the drug industry or the ethical pharmaceutical industry. I have dealt with this matter a number of times in the past, and recently a fair amount of publicity has been given to the activities of the Kefauver committee in the United States and also the statement of evidence by the director of the branch to the restrictive trade practices commission.
I should like to refer briefly to an article by Charles King which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of December 11, 1959, in which he deals with certain statements by

Mr. Stanley Conder of the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers' association with regard to the prices of certain types of drugs, an exchange of comments between myself and Mr. Conder through the newspapers and statements I made in the house.
I want to point out first that the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers' association, according to the latest information I have, has some 60 pharmaceutical houses or companies affiliated with it and represents, by its own statement, 90 per cent of the industry in Canada. Mr. Conder made some comments about the profit picture of the Canadian industry. He pointed out that the average profit after taxes was 6.5 per cent which he said was "not out of line with the general economy".
The difficulty, of course, in dealing with whether or not that is a correct figure is that a large number of the drug companies in Canada are subsidiaries of United States parent companies primarily or in some cases of companies in other lands. Therefore the Canadian financial picture is hidden in the annual reports of the parent company and is not shown as a separate item, so it is not possible to deal with that particular point.
I would say that the drug industry of Canada is controlled primarily by parent companies in the United States although some of the parent companies are in Switzerland, the United Kingdom or France. Primarily though it is the United States drug industry which controls the drug industry in Canada. Therefore I think we are entitled to draw some comparisons between the industry in the United States in the light of its examination by various public bodies and the industry in Canada.
In June of 1958 the federal trade commission of the United States published what it called an economic report on antibiotics manufacturing which deals with profits in the industry. I wish to make only a passing reference to it before dealing with the Canadian industry. On page 216 there is a table showing the net profit as a percentage of assets for certain antibiotic and other pharmaceutical manufacturers from 1950 to 1956. In it are named the companies and figures are set out for their pharmaceutical operations as distinguished from their antibiotic operations, and as separated from the total consolidated financial picture if indeed proprietary medicines were dealt with also. It shows so far as pharmaceutical operations are concerned, under profits as a percentage of assets for the year 1960, that the company of Smith, Kline and French had a percentage profit of 74.5. I mention this company because it has a Canadian subsidiary. G. D. Searle and Company had a profit of 55.04 per cent.
Supply-Justice
That company also has a Canadian subsidiary. Schering Corporation Limited had a profit of 50 per cent. There are other companies listed here but I picked those three out because they are parent companies in the United States with subsidiaries in Canada. The weighted average for 10 companies is 37 per cent, which is an increase of 10 percentage points over the picture in 1950 for the same companies, increasing from 26.3 per cent in 1950 to 37.5 per cent in 1956.
In Canada, as I say, it is a bit more difficult to pick out these particular figures. However, there are some figures available. With respect to the various companies, although not necessarily in this order, I mention the companies involved: Abbott Laboratories Limited; Ames Co. of Canada; Ayerst, McKenna and Harrison; Bristol Laboratories; British Drug Houses; Burroughs Wellcome & Co.; Canada Pharmacal Co.; Ciba Co. Ltd.; Cyanamid of Canada; Dymond; Charles E. Frosst; Hoffman-La Roche Ltd.; Frank W. Horner Ltd.; Eli Lilly Co.; Merck & Co.; Parke-Davis & Co.; Pfizer Corp.; Pitman-Moore of Canada; Poulenc; Riker Pharmaceutical Co.; Schering Corp.; G. D. Searle & Co.; Smith, Kline & French Inter-American Corp.; E. R. Squibb & Sons; Upjohn Co. of Canada; Winthrop Laboratories of Canada; and John Wyeth. Of these companies 18 are subsidiaries of United States parent companies. I am afraid there is no date on this particular publication, of the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers' association but I received it some time last year. So at least as of last year all but four of the companies I last mentioned were members of the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers' association, and that is what is shown with respect to the profit picture of the Canadian industry.

From this we find that the pharmaceutical industry in Canada has the second highest profit rate, being second only to the paper products industry. From this I think we can therefore conclude that the situation is not, as the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers said it was or claimed, namely that their profit picture is not out of line with the general economy. I should like to deal with the argument advanced by the pharmaceutical industry that its high prices are justified and necessary on the ground that the industry makes extensive and large expenditures in the field of research and must recoup these expenditures on research as quickly as they can before the drug itself is replaced by some more efficacious drug made by another company or by the same company, and that they spend on research many dollars which result in nothing usable being developed. I think this argument about extensive expenditures on research is not a factual one and is not one of the major reasons why there are such high prices in the drug industry as I intend to show.
Again referring to the United States and their federal trade commission economic report on antibiotics for 1958 at page 205, we find some statistical information given by the federal trade commission. In this instance they do not identify the companies by name but merely designate them as company No. 1, company No. 2 and so on. For the period 1956, so far as salary and advertising expenses are concerned-and I will deal with this part of it first-as a percentage of the sales dollars, company No. 1 expended on selling and advertising 26.4 per cent of its sales dollars. Company No. 2 in the line expended 24 per cent on selling and advertising. On company No. 3 there is no information available. Company No. 4 expended 28.1 per cent; No. 5, 14.4 per cent; No. 6, 30.7 per cent; for No. 7, No. 8 and No. 9 there is no information available; No. 10, expended 14.4 per cent; No. 11, 14.6 per cent; No. 12, 8.5 per cent.
With respect to Canada the picture is somewhat the same. Without going into a long series of statistics about each of the companies I mentioned earlier I would say this.

The average of all the companies I mentioned earlier is not quite 25 per cent. That is the percentage of their sales dollar which is expended on advertising, salesmen, detail men, direct mailings, supplying samples and the like. Perhaps I should give the committee the exact figure; it is considered that 24.93 per cent of the sales dollar is expended on selling, advertising, research, and so on.
If we calculate this in relation to the cost of goods sold by these companies, we find this averages out at 36.21 per cent. I think anyone would agree that this is a particularly high percentage of the sales dollar income to be expended on selling, advertising and promotional activities of the industry. I will relate this to research expenditures in a moment or two.
This matter has also concerned the Canadian medical association and is referred to in the Canadian medical association journal of September 3, 1960. At page 505 we find a portion of the report of the committee on pharmacy of the Canadian medical association, which reads as follows:
The cost of drugs has been a matter of much discussion in recent months. There is no doubt that the pharmaceutical houses have made many contributions in past years to our ability to alleviate illnesses which in the aggregate represent an almost incalculable economic and humanistic gain to our community. There is some evidence to suggest that the return which they are receiving on their original investment is excessive.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member what he is reading from?
This is a reference in the Canadian medical association journal of September 3, 1960; it is volume 83, page 505.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the document from which my hon. friend is reading now?
No, this is an excerpt taken from the Canadian medical association journal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am wondering what document my hon. friend is reading from, if he would be kind enough to say.

I am reading from a document, page 118, called "Material collected for submission to the restrictive trade practices commission in the course of an inquiry under section 42 of the Combines Investigation Act relating to the manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs by director of investigation and research Combines Investigation Act, Department of Justice, Ottawa, 1961".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for giving me the information. I have to raise a point of order. The hon. member is reading from a report on material obtained by the director of investigation and

research and transmitted by him to the restrictive trade practices commission.
On a number of occasions recently motions have been made in this house by the hon. member who has just spoke calling for the production of this report and the production of various documents that were before the director in the course of compiling his report. The house has decided that these documents should not be produced, and the motions in every case have been rejected by the house.
I recognize that some portions of this document, copies of which were supplied by the chairman of the restrictive trade practices commission to parties and persons whom the commission thought it might be appropriate to ask to appear before it, have found their way into the hands of the press. It is alleged that portions of them have been reproduced in the press.
However, I raise the point of order that in so far as proceedings or discussions in this committee at this time are concerned, it would not be proper to attempt to introduce any portion of that report, from wherever it may come, whether by reading from the report itself or by reading alleged portions thereof which have been reproduced in the press.
I take my position on that point of order on the basis of section 28 of the Combines Investigation Act, which says:
All Inquiries under this act shall be conducted in private, except that the chairman of the commission may order that all or any portion of any proceedings before the commission or any member thereof shall be conducted in public.
The house has taken the position that this is a document which should be kept private, and it is therefore not open to me, and I submit it is not open to any hon. member of the house or this committee, to seek to discuss that report or to attempt to introduce any portion of it into the record.
If it be argued by the hon. member that this position is not consistent, that a portion of a report which has been reproduced in the press and may therefore be read by hon. members of the house outside the house should not be excluded from proceedings in the house, my answer is that the only purpose for which these portions of the report could be read here must be for the purpose of discussing the report. Since the discussion of the report is in my submission out of order, it is not appropriate or in order to read the report or portions of it at this stage. I point out further, sir, that it seems to me to be a matter of judgment or, to use the words in May's Parliamentary Practice, a matter of "good taste" as to the extent to which a private member is permitted to read from documents which cannot be produced in the house.
Supply-Justice
In that connection may I emphasize that the report of the director, while it is impartial in so far as the director is concerned- his task in this kind of inquiry is not to make a case for or against any individual or group of individuals, but to report what he finds and his conclusions thereon and lay that report before the commission-at this stage it is a one-sided report because the parties had not been given the opportunity to present their cases in full.
When the time comes for the commission to hold its hearings, the commission, with the director's report before it, copies of which are supplied to the parties, invites the parties to make their comments. Then the commission's report is of course made public and at that stage we have a balanced report; the case on both sides is summarized.
The second ground of my point of order is the matter of the propriety or, as May says, "good taste" in permitting reference to this kind of document which, as I have said, is a one-sided document at this stage.
The scheme and purpose of the Combines Investigation Act, as appears so clearly in section 28 which I have read, is that inquiries by the director should be private and nothing should be published unless and until the chairman of the restrictive trade practices commission, in his sole discretion, decides that the hearings before his commission should be in public; otherwise nothing is published until the commission makes its report. Then, by the statute, that report is required to be made public.
At this stage, therefore, with respect to the report of the director it is my submission that it is not in order to read from it or to read purported extracts from it, because it is not a document which can properly be before the House of Commons at this stage, and the house on three separate occasions in the very recent past has so decided.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to point out with respect to this particular document that it is true a motion was made and the house rejected the motion to table a document called a report of the director regarding the pricing and selling policies of certain pharmaceutical houses in respect of new types of drugs, if I recall the words correctly. I have used them so often recently that they are almost as familiar as my own name. It is correct that the House of Commons decided it should not be tabled, but I submit, with respect, that this decision under which the Minister of Justice was not required to table the document does not prevent any hon. member reading from that particular document.

Supply-Justice
We hear continually in this chamber hon. members reading from correspondence and documents of a like nature which are considered to be private. Some years ago a famous debate arose about horses on the payroll. That involved a private document, yet references were made to it and extracts were read from it by various members, including members of the Tory party. There is no ground for a point of order being raised here. I am not infringing any rule of the committee, unless it be said that I am reading a speech, but I would point out that I endorse the point of view expressed in whatever observations I do read, and, in any case, I am not reading from the report of the director himself but from a photostatic copy of that report, if hon. members want to get technical about it, reproduced in a publication which is in the public domain.
Not long ago-I believe it was a week ago Wednesday-the House of Commons agreed to a motion of mine-and the parliamentary secretary to the minister said it was fine and dandy-that a list of documents and publications to which the public has access, with bibliographic reference to material perused or used by the combines investigation branch should be produced, and this is undoubtedly one of the published documents used or perused by the combines investigation branch. As I say, the house has already ordered that we should be furnished with such a list together with bibliographic references. The only condition attached to it was that it was not to be taken that any publication so listed or any of the bibliographic references were necessarily contained in the report itself.
All I am doing in this instance is to read from a document entitled the Canadian medical association journal. The public has access to this particular publication, and I am reading from it, even though the actual words are not written by the journal itself but are reproduced from it. I submit, on these grounds, that there is no substance in the point of order.

I should like to make a few comments on this point of order, but before I proceed to do so may I take this opportunity to express the hope that the hon. member for Spadina, the assistant Deputy Speaker, will soon be able to return to this house. I mention this not because you are in the chair, sir, but simply because I happen to have visited the hon. member yesterday. While I express this hope, I want you to know, sir, that we have every confidence in the person who is occupying the chair at this moment.

I rise to support the position taken by the hon. member for Skeena. The votes which have taken place in this house are not involved in this particular dispute. The house has voted on three different occasions that the minister should not be required to produce the particular report in question, nor should he be required to table it. That is not the point at issue at the present time. The minister quotes, in support of the position he takes, section 28 of the Combines Investigation Act which reads as follows:
All Inquiries under this act shall be conducted in private, except that the chairman of the commission may order that all or any portion of any proceedings before the commission or any member thereof shall be conducted in public.
That section does not in any way affect the nature of the dispute between the hon. member for Skeena and the Minister of Justice. That section deals with the in camera character of the proceedings of the commission. It does not preclude any publication of the proceedings of the commission, and certainly it in no way affects this committee of supply. It is a provision which is confined entirely to enquiries held under this act.
The document in question has been made public as a result of action taken by the chairman of the commission-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not right.
Am I wrong in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would take issue with it. This was made public, apparently, by some of those to whom the commission had sent it on a private basis.

I accept the correction. However, it was put in the hands of a number of people and it became a public document and was referred to in the press. Now the minister has taken the position that a document which is at the present time, in its essentials, public property, cannot be referred to in this committee by the hon. member for Skeena, that it cannot be dealt with in the way in which he is endeavouring to deal with at least part of the report. I cannot agree with the contention advanced by the minister. I think the hon. member is perfectly justified in discussing in this public forum a report which is now public property, and it would seem to be that for the minister to take the attitude he does is unusual, particularly if we bear in mind that on another occasion the Prime Minister had no hesitation in disclosing in this house what admittedly was a secret document, namely the so-called economic report which he revealed so brazenly in 1958.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And tabled.

And which he had tabled; a confidential document, a document which had not been the property of the public. But the Prime Minister had no hesitation in taking that confidential document and using it for the purpose which served him at that particular moment.
The hon. member is referring here to something which has become a matter of public concern and public knowledge. This being the case, he seeks to take advantage of the fact by discussing in this chamber what he could go out and discuss in any public hall at any time. If the hon. member were to take this report and go down to the Chateau Laurier and call a public meeting in the ballroom to discuss this report, no one could stop him. Yet because of milieu in which we find ourselves, he is denied the opportunity to do something he could do at any time outside this chamber. If the Minister of Justice seeks to set aside my argument on the ground that he can not be compelled to table the report, I say that the decision of this house was not that the report should not be discussed but simply that the minister should not be compelled to produce it. That was the decision which was made, and it is defensible, although I do not myself agree with it. It is defensible because the minister is the minister to whom the chairman of the commission is responsible. He argues that in these circumstances the position he must take in respect of these matters until they reach finality is a neutral position. That would be a legitimate argument for the minister to use in connection with the production of a document and it was, in a sense, the argument which he did use at the time. But it does not in any way affect this situation and the right of the hon. member for Skeena.
So, Mr. Chairman, I suggest to you that it is clear that the hon. gentleman should be allowed to discuss this report just as much as he would be allowed to discuss it outside this house, and just as much as editorial writers, radio commentators and others are discussing this report, which has come to them, in the way which we have already mentioned it has come to the public. For those reasons I strongly support the position taken by the hon. member for Skeena.

Mr. Chairman, in the consideration which I asked the committee to give to the point of order raised, I ask the committee and you to include this fact. At page 460 of May's sixteenth edition, it is stated that a minister may not cite a paper or document which he is not prepared to table. If, then the situation is that it is not proper to table a document, a minister is unable to discuss it. Therefore I am in a position where I am unable to discuss this document, for I think it is quite clear that I would be in breach of the spirit as well as the letter of the statute which I am responsible to administer if I were to discuss this document at this time.
I am precluded from discussing it, as May has pointed out at page 460 and page 461. I suggest hon. members are also in this position, although greater latitude has been permitted in this regard to members than to ministers of the crown.
Since, in my view, this document should not be tabled because it is private, and the house has supported that principle by its decision, it seems to me the hon. member should not discuss it. Whether he does or not, I cannot discuss it, and it seems to me, therefore, that the committee and you, Mr. Chairman, should give some consideration to the question as to whether it is in accord with the rules and customs of this house that reference should be made to an extract from a document which should not be discussed, and which I cannot answer during the consideration of my estimates.
Consideration should also be given to the principle of good taste, quite apart from the fact that the report itself at this stage does not present a full picture, but only one side. Is it proper that an hon. member, into whose possession a photostatic copy of this document has come, should be permitted to discuss it when it is not a matter which I am able to discuss in the consideration of my estimates at this stage? That is the third reason, in my submission, why this document should not be read into the record or tabled before this house at this time. To discuss it at this time, I submit, would result in a one-sided presentation, and I suggest the committee should ask itself very carefully whether that would be proper. In addition

Supply-Justice
to that, I suggest it is not in order for an hon. member to read from a document which cannot be tabled.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one statement regarding-
I recognize the hon. member for Skeena.

Mr. Chairman, apart from the suggestions made before, I feel the minister is raising another consideration under this point of order, and is in reality prejudging his own decision of some future date. He has said on this occasion, as well as on at least one other occasion in this house, that the report of the restrictive trade practices commission will be made public. I suggest that is not necessarily the case. The act gives the minister the authority to make that report public if he deems it in the public interest to do so. I should just like to correct him in that regard. The minister at this stage is not in a position to prejudge his own opinion in regard to a report which has not been completed, and which he has not seen as yet. I suggest his statement in respect of tabling the report should be qualified to the extent that, if within 30 days of the time the report is completed he deems to make it advisable to make it public, it will become public.

Mr. Chairman, when the minister referred to the citation from May, he did not identify it, and I was not, therefore, in a position to understand it. Since that time the Solicitor General has sent me a copy of the sixteenth edition of May. While I do not complain about anything the minister has read from May, I think it is important that the concluding paragraph in May under the title "Citing Documents Not Before the House" ought to be placed before Your Honour. That paragraph reads as follows:
Members not connected with the government have also cited documents in their possession, both public and private, which were not before the house:
Therefore, there is-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. member read the rest of the paragraph?

I intended to and I shall. I suggest, therefore, there is strong precedent for what the hon. gentleman has done today.

As the Minister of Justice has requested, I shall read the rest of that paragraph, which is as follows:
-but though the house is equally unable to form a correct judgment from partial extracts-
That is what we have today. I continue:
-inconvenient latitude has sometimes been permitted, which it is doubtful whether any rule but that of good taste could have restrained.
The matter is not laid obviously to a decision of the Chair, because there is no rule that has been contravened as a result of the action taken by the hon. member. I simply repeat that what the hon. gentleman has done today, any persons outside this house could do, and are doing now through different agencies of one kind or another.

I should like the minister to assist me in respect of one point. At page 500 of Votes and Proceedings there appears a motion of the hon. member for Skeena for the production of specific documents. I should like the minister to confirm my impression, that the motion which appears there has regard to this particular report?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, the motion of the hon. member for Skeena was, that an order of the house do issue for a copy of the statement of evidence by the combines investigation branch regarding the selling and pricing policies of certain pharmaceutical houses in respect of certain new types of drugs. The vote of the house in respect of that motion was 37 in favour and 148 against, as reported in Hansard of May 3, 1961. This is the document to which that motion referred.
Perhaps I may take the advantage of this moment to say one or two more things in this regard. I rest my case on the matter of good taste, as covered in the passage from May, as read by the hon. member for Essex East. My case in this regard is, whether it is in good taste to read from a document in light of the fact that all we can get is a onesided presentation in respect of which I am not at liberty to participate in the discussion.

document no longer existed, and therefore no objection could be taken to its being tabled. Therefore, that document was properly laid before this house.
That document continues to be confidential.

Mr. Chairman, in respect of the point raised by the minister, I should like to suggest that I am trying to present a one-sided case; the people's side. I do not advance this as having any actual bearing on your ruling, Mr. Chairman, or on the point of order, but I would point out there is some doubt whether the document from which I am reading is actually the document with which the motion dealt. I do not think it is particularly important because, if I can quote it correctly, the motion referred to the statement of evidence by the director of investigation and research regarding the selling and pricing policies of certain pharmaceutical houses in respect of new types of drugs. I have not it exactly before me but I think I have given the gist of the motion.
I have not a statement of evidence before me. What I am quoting from to identify the document for the minister is "Material collected for submission to the restrictive trade practices commission in the course of an inquiry under section 42 of the Combines Investigation Act relating to the manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs by director of investigation and research, Combines Investigation Act, Department of Justice, Ottawa, 1961". The comparable words are "the director of investigation and research". These words are mentioned both in the motion and on the front page of this particular document. This does not mention certain pharmaceutical houses, as does the motion. In the identifying sheet it makes no reference to certain pharmaceutical houses. The document I have here does not relate to what are known as new types of drugs. It refers to the manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs.
May I emphasize this in another way and refer to what is known as the preface dated February 28, 1961, signed by D. H. W. Henry, director of investigation and research. To avoid any misunderstanding may I emphasize that this is not a report under the Combines Investigation Act. It is a statement of material collected and analysed by the director of investigation and research for the purpose of being laid before the restrictive trade practices commission in the course of an inquiry under section 42 of the act. The text of section 42 is set out on page 1 of the statement and provides that the commission is required:
... to consider any evidence or material brought before it... together with such further evidence or material as the commission considers advisable and to report thereon In writing to the minister.
