The preface goes on to talk about the present director's predecessor, Mr. MacDonald, and so on, but nowhere is there any reference to certain pharmaceutical houses or to new types of drugs nor to the selling and pricing policies of certain houses but merely to the manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs. I cited this only because a question was raised whether this was the matter referred to in the motion which I submit is not too relevant, anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is perfectly clear that this is the only report prepared by the director. Its correct title is, "Statement of Material". It is the only document that he has placed before the commission, and by one of the sections of the act this investigation is made an inquiry, and that is what is referred to in section 28 as the thing which should be conducted in private. All inquiries are to be conducted in private. This is the only document. I do not think my hon. friend from Skeena really quarrels with my suggestion that all of us all along have known that this is the document which was the subject matter of the motion which was placed before the house on an earlier occasion.

I start with the premise that the Chair is under the control of the house. On Wednesday, May 3, a motion for the production of a report, which I am satisfied has been identified as this report or part of a larger report, was rejected by a vote of 148 to 37. Therefore, this puts the minister in the position where any reference by the hon. member to this report cannot be commented on by the minister. I refer the committee to Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, citation 159 (2), which reads:
A minister of the crown is not at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or other state paper not before the house, unless he is prepared to lay it upon the table. This restraint is similar to the rule of evidence in courts of law, which prevent counsel from citing documents which have not been produced in evidence.
I take it that the point made with respect to the matter of not being in good taste is something which is also worthy of consideration. I go back to my original point that the Chair is in the hands of the house. On an earlier occasion the house came to a decision and accordingly I must rule that any reference to the document by the hon. member concerned is out of order.

Mr. Chairman, you are coming to the conclusion that the document from which I am reading is the same document which the house said would not be tabled. The minister may think it is but I for one do not. However, I shall abide by your ruling

Supply-Justice
and I will not quote from the document itself in the house, although I gather I am at liberty to quote from it outside, if I so desire, as well as anyone else who wishes to do so.
If the minister is at a disadvantage now in being unable to table the document I have no objection at all to tabling it. I make it available freely to anyone. I will table it and the minister will be at liberty to discuss something that is before the house.
In any event, I would point out with respect to the high expenditures of the drug industry on selling and advertising, this has been of great concern to the Canadian medical association. At its annual meeting last year the Canadian medical association received a report from one of its committees, I believe the committee on pharmacy, and this report referred to the excessive charges of the pharmaceutical manufacturing industry. The committee on pharmacy of the Canadian medical association was of the opinion that far too much expenditure was being made by the pharmaceutical industry, in selling, in promotional advertising and in gimmicks such as recordings and the like with a nursery rhyme on one side and a plug for one particular brand of pharmaceutical on the other. All of the other costs such as reproduction of oil paintings, paper weights, pencils, knives, office material and the like are considered by many members of the medical profession and by the association to contribute toward the high cost of drugs and to constitute one of the main reasons why high prices are charged to the consumers.
With reference to the expenditures on research, I should like to refer to a document which is in the public domain. It is published by the federal trade commission of the United States. I refer to the economic report on antibiotics manufacture. I would point out that in substance there is no difference whatsoever between the federal trade commission report in the United States in so far as its connection with companies and the like are concerned and the particular document to which I referred and which you ruled, Mr. Chairman, I could not use. This is precisely the same kind of document. Apparently in the United States it is O.K. to have these things made public but we want to be a bit more secretive in Canada.
Let us look at the expenditures on selling and advertising of some of the companies mentioned. Company No. 1 spent 8.1 per cent on research. The committee will remember that earlier I said it spent 26.4 per cent on selling and advertising. It spent three times as much on selling and advertising as it did on research. Company No. 2 spent 3.9 per cent on research and 24 per cent on selling

and advertising. In other words, the amount of money spent on selling and advertising was more than six times the amount spent on research. For company No. 3 the information is not available. Company No. 4 spent 7.9 per cent on research compared with 28.1 per cent on selling and advertising. Over three times as much was spent on promotional gimmicks and through expense accounts and so on as was spent on research.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Would the hon. member agree that a great deal of the cost of selling and advertising is absorbed by the wages of salesmen?

What my friend is now doing is asking me to refer to a document to which I am prohibited from making reference. My information is taken from the report of the federal trade commission and all I can say is that there is no differentiation made between salesmen's wages and so on. It is all lumped together as selling and advertising, and I am not able to answer that question by referring to this document. If you would agree to reverse your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and allow me to refer to this other document, I could give that information without any difficulty.
What is the picture in Canada? The picture in Canada is that in the main the pharmaceutical industry spends practically nothing on research. In company after company what is the percentage of the sales dollar that is spent on research? One per cent, 1J per cent, If per cent. For the 27 companies I mentioned earlier an average of 1.21 per cent of the sales dollar is spent on research compared with approximately 25 per cent spent on selling and advertising.
They also claim that expenditure is necessary for what they call quality control to ensure that the consumer gets the best possible type of product, that the product is of the purest quality and the most efficacious in the treatment of the ailment for which it is prescribed. Again, the Canadian pharmaceutical industry spends in some instances three quarters of 1 per cent of the sales dollar on quality control. Some of the companies spend nothing on quality control. The average is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 1 per cent of the sales dollar which is spent on quality control. If I may quote again from the December 11, 1959, issue of the Ottawa Citizen, this is what Stanley Conder of the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers' association says is "a very, very costly proposition". Approximately 1 cent of the sales dollar goes into quality control to ensure that the public is protected and gets the purest drugs. One cent is spent

to ensure the safety of the public while 25 cents is spent by the manufacturers to ensure that they bamboozle the doctors into remembering the particular brand name of a pharmaceutical.
There is another phase to this matter with respect to why this situation has come about. Hon. members will recall that I mentioned that our drug industry is controlled by the drug industry of the United States. The patent picture also shows that is the case. I should like to make reference to the patents held by the United States companies if I may. I have here an order for return which is referred to in Votes and Proceedings No. 30, page 195, for February 24, 1960. I had asked who held certain patents and there are 15 pages of information here. There is no need to go into them extensively. I would point out that in each and every instance the patents for the so-called wonder drugs or antibiotics are held by the parent companies in the United States regardless of whether or not they have Canadian subsidiaries. I note that Merck and Company, for instance, of Rahway, New Jersey, holds a total of 30 patents on the drug or pharmaceutical known as streptomycin. Charles Pfizer and Company of Brooklyn, New York, holds nine patents on the same drug. When it comes to tetracycline, one of the broad spectrum antibiotics and an important base for a lot of these drugs, Charles Pfizer and Company of Brooklyn holds nine patents, American Cyanamid of New York holds 18 patents, Bristol Laboratories of East Syracuse, New York, holds five patents, and so on.
All the way down the line, for pharmaceutical after pharmaceutical the control is concentrated in the hands of these companies in the United States. Because of patent control, which puts the company holding the patent in somewhat of a monopoly position, these companies are able to charge higher rates for their products than they normally would.
I should like to place on the record some figures giving a comparison of prices paid by the Department of Defence Production in purchases it has made with the prices that the consumer has to pay for the same drug. This information was given in answer to questions of mine during the last session of parliament. I do not have the return with me but it is easily obtainable by reference to the Journals of the house. I should like to give one or two examples of the cost to the Department of Defence Production compared with what the consumer has to pay.
At the top of the list there is a drug known as tyrothricin with benzocaine lozenges. The manufacturer is Merck, Sharpe and
Supply-Justice
Dohme and the brand name under which the consumer buys the product is tyrozets. In October, 1959, the Department of Defence Production paid 22 cents per vial of 12 for these lozenges while the cost to the consumer was $1, or almost five times as much. The difference between the retail price and the price paid by the Department of Defence Production for this same pharmaceutical or drug is 454.5 per cent at the retail level and 272.7 per cent at the wholesale level.
You can go down the list and pick out others that are used regularly and which show precisely the same picture. Perhaps I might refer to one that has been in the news recently because of the activity of the food and drug directorate in issuing some suggestions about its possible misuse. I refer to a drug called chloramphenicol. It is a Parke Davis preparation and its brand name is Chloromycetin. In November, 1959, the Department of Defence Production purchased this product at a price of $11.25 for 100, 250 milligram tablets. The cost to the consumer for the same pharmaceutical was $56.70 per 100 tablets. This is a retail difference of 504 per cent or 302 per cent at the wholesale level.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to mention all of those that are shown here but I would point out that substantially the same picture is evident throughout. The difference ranges from 200 per cent to 400 per cent or 520 per cent.

Here is another example I point out in order to show that there are differences in price and that it is possible to sell these pharmaceuticals at a lower price. If I may, I want to refer to the federal trade commission economic report on antibiotics manufacture of 1958. At page 192 there is a table headed: "Broad Spectrum Antibiotic Prices-46 250-milligram capsules". These are of the same class of drugs. I think this is an important table to which to refer, Mr. Chairman, in so far as the United States is concerned. As I said,

Supply-Justice
because of their corporate control and their patent control the Canadian picture is influenced to a great extent or perhaps almost exclusively by the picture of these companies in the United States.
At September 27, 1951, according to the reference here, a drug called terramycin was sold in the United States to the retailer at the price of $5.10 for 16 capsules and was sold to the consumer at the price of $8.50 for 16 capsules and that situation continued from then on in October, 1951; November, 1953; April, 1954; September, 1954; October, 1954; December, 1955; and December, 1956. It is shown during those same months to which I have just referred that other similar types of broad spectrum antibiotics entered the market at exactly the same price or were sold to the retailer at $5.10 and at $8.50 to the consumer. The report lists these drugs by their names. I think the conclusion to which we can come is that since September 27, 1951, the price range has not varied one penny even though there have been tremendous increases in sales of this type of antibiotics Even though other companies entered the field with the same sort of antibiotic under a different brand name, they entered the market at the same price that was established as of September 27, 1951. This will lead one to believe that there is relatively little room for price differentials or competition to take place at least in the broad spectrum antibiotic field. I think all this leads us to assess what this means in terms of a consumer in Canada. How about the individual who has a prescription in his hands and walks into the drug store? How is he concerned or how is he affected by the activities of the drug industry?
I wanted to be able to put into the record a bit more information in this particular field so it would not appear that it was in bad taste, as the minister said. However, I am now prevented from doing that and attempting to balance the picture out, even though I think the document I have here is not the one to which the minister referred. The names are certainly different on it. But in any event, I am prevented from doing that, Mr. Chairman. Nevertheless I think there are certain conclusions that can be drawn in a general way. I think this is advantageous because this matter requires some public discussion, in my opinion; and the more public discussion there is about it, the more possibility I believe there is of drug prices declining. Some newspapers in the country have conducted surveys in this regard, and with respect to some types or classes of pharmaceuticals in the ethical pharmaceutical industry there have been reductions in prices within the last year and a half or two years, whereas

for some considerable time previously there were no reductions in prices. I found this statement to be substantiated by having talked with two separate individuals who are pharmacists and whom I know. They also pointed out that they have noticed this fact in the various price lists they get from time to time from the pharmaceutical concerns, namely that in the last year and a half or thereabouts, so far as some drugs are concerned, there has been a decline in the price charged by the manufacturer.
I am sure that this is to a large extent the result of the activities of the Kefauver committee in the United States and the publicity that has been attached to the inquiry that has been conducted in Canada by the combines investigation branch, and the attendant publicity that was given to some of the material contained in that particular statement of evidence.
I think my time is running short at the moment. Rather than proceed to deal with my conclusions drawn from the information I have been able to obtain, perhaps I should leave my remarks stand there at the moment. There may be another opportunity, following the comments of other members who are interested in this field or a statement by the minister, for me to rise and draw some conclusions from some of the things that have been said.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been a little reluctant to be drawn in, as it were, as third man in this combination which has reminded me of the old combination of Tinker to Evans to Chance. In this case it has been from Skeena to Timiskaming and back to Skeena again.
However, I think I should make a few comments, if only for the purpose of pointing out that at this stage there is nothing I can say about this drug inquiry for reasons which I indicated in the course of the discussion of the point of order.
The matter has been looked into by the director. A lengthy document has been presented by him to the commission and the matter is now before the commission for hearing. Not only, then, is it improper for me to discuss anything which is contained in the director's statement of material, but I think it would be untimely for us to make a decision now and for me to attempt to tell the committee what conclusions the government has arrived at and what it intends to do,

Supply-Justice
because we are not yet in possession of the report which will ultimately be provided to us in accordance with the provisions of the act. I refer to the report of the commission. This report will be provided when all the inquiries and hearings have been concluded.
At that time I hope and expect we will receive a report that will be helpful, based on the complete study which the act contemplates, and not on a partial consideration, which is all we have before us at the present time. We naturally would be expected to look into the matter in the meantime and I can assure the committee that this is being done, to see if there emerges from what is now available anything that really indicates that something could be done in the federal field without waiting for a further report.
There may be one or two particular aspects where the results of our consideration may suggest courses of action, but these, I submit, would be of an interim nature. Before it would be sensible for us to make up our minds as to the comprehensive action we should take, surely we should wait until we receive the over-all report which covers the whole field.
Certainly these inquiries take a long time. I am not happy about this; no one is happy about it, but they are pressed with all dispatch in the light of other work and other inquiries which come before both the director and the commission. I have not in my possession the information as to the actual length of time taken by the F.T.C. study in the United States, but it is my impression that it was a lengthy study. Certainly the committee in the United States of which Senator Kefauver is head has been working for at least two years and there has been as yet no full report. Indeed, I understand that in the United States nothing by way of executive action has emerged even as yet from the F.T.C. report, with the exception, I believe, of one prosecution in connection with Salk vaccine.
As will be appreciated, the situation in this country with respect to Salk vaccine is not at all the same as it is in the United States. The prices of Salk vaccine are pretty well controlled by the fact that the Connaught laboratory is at least the prime mover in the field although it does not actually control the whole field.
And the institute of microbiology of Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Essex East reminds me that the institute of microbiology of Montreal is also engaged in that field. I say this not in the way of boasting of the fact that these inquiries take this long,
tMr. Fulton.]
but simply to ask hon. members to realize that a proper sense of proportion suggests that inquiries of this kind in other countries as well as in Canada are necessarily time consuming, and even after they are concluded it is not possible to take startling and widespread action in a matter of days or weeks. We shall, however, be looking forward with interest to the report of the commission, at which time we shall be able to ascertain what action it is proper to take to deal with whatever problem is outlined in the over-all field and, I repeat, if in the interim a study of the material now available enables me to make any useful recommendation to my colleagues as to what could be done on an interim basis I shall do that, and I have arranged that the material should be studied, from that point of view. This study is going on now.

Before this item carries, may I say I can appreciate that these matters do take a considerable period of time to examine and study. Perhaps other hon. members will now appreciate why it sometimes takes a long time to talk about this in the House of Commons.

speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member will permit a question. speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Steady, now. Hold yourself to the point.

-when one of its
ministers rises to complain about the participation in the debate by a private member of this house.
He only asked a question.

The hon. member against whom the complaint has been made does not belong to my party, but I believe so strongly in the value of this house that I would fight for the rights of any member, including private members supporting the government, and for the minister to complain because an hon. member has discharged his responsibility as he sees it, is, I contend, an indication of the increased arrogance of a government which is growing in public disfavour.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is a lot of nonsense. I was making no complaint about the hon. member exercising his right to speak. I was speaking on behalf of the other members of this committee who should have the opportunity to take part in a discussion of the estimates of this department.

Yes. I cannot help it if the minister's supporters are hesitant and bashful in approaching these matters and if they do not want to engage in an examination of the workings of the department. If the minister wants to have a bunch of silent Sams or rubber stamps behind him, that is for him to decide.
There are no rubber stamps behind the minister.
What did the Prime Minister say the other day about inveterate babblers? In any event it applies to the hon. member for Saskatoon, I can say that.
On a point of order, I think the hon. member should withdraw the statement that we are a bunch of rubber stamps. It is not true.

I think that there is a certain amount of special concern attaching to the activities of the retail pharmacists within the pharmaceutical industry. The retail pharmacists are, of course, subjected to the largest degree of complaint by the general public, a great deal of which is unjustified. This arises because the retail pharmacist is the individual with whom the consumer deals.
On a point of order I do not believe retail pharmacists come within the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice.
Where have you been all day?
I have been here longer than you have.
You have not.

I say that this complaint is registered against the retail pharmacists because they are the individuals with whom
Supply-Justice
the consumer deals. He sees his fifteen or twenty dollars passed across the counter, in exchange for which he gets a small bottle or vial of tablets or cream or lotion. There is an activity in the retail field which does,
I	think, give rise to concern and contributes to the high cost of drugs. I should like to cite two examples. I refer, first, to a prescription which was given for aspirin, ordinary aspirin which anyone can buy. The purchase price of aspirin on this prescription, which was supplied here in Ottawa, was 50 cents. Without a prescription aspirin costs 32 cents. This is an indication of the effect of what is known as a prescription fee within the pharmaceutical industry. I have been told by others of an instance in which some tablets were sold by prescription at $1.15 a dozen, or a total cost of $9.90 a hundred. When sold by the hundred without prescription, because they are not an ethical drug, the selling price is $1.85. This represents a difference of some $8.00 and indicates another contributing factor to the high cost of drugs in this country.
In addition to that there is, of course, an
II	per cent sales tax on drugs, and on some items a tariff is applicable also. I think in essence we can say that in relation to the sale of drugs in Canada patents have been and are being used to create monopolistic situations which Canadian law appears to have been designed to prevent and the control exercised over the manufacture, distribution and sale of certain drugs through patents has virtually eliminated price competition in respect to these drugs and has encouraged other forms of competition. These, while possibly bringing other benefits to the public have resulted in prices being increased rather than decreased. Practices which are quite legal and unobjectionable in themselves- promotion, use of trade names and the like- appear to have been carried to extremes because of the insulation of certain sectors of the industry from price competition by reason of the control exercised through patents.
As is indicated below, the effects of the control exercised through patents affect the prices of certain drugs only. On the other hand, the practices of retail druggists affect the prices of all products sold in drug stores. These practices have resulted in the virtual elimination of price competition at the retail level.
Prices of drugs in Canada are among the highest in the world. These prices tend to reflect current prices of the same or comparative drug products in the United States, but because of the sales tax applicable in Canada prices to consumers in Canada are about 11 per cent higher.

Supply-Justice
The general information that we have indicates that prices of proprietary drug products are not unduly high in any sense, and I refer to those that are not included in the ethical drug field. Also, an established brand which has wide public acceptance is normally sold at a premium price. There are numerous substitutes available, and the consumer has a wide choice of products at various price levels. It is obvious that, because of considerations of health and personal well being, brand name product preference is likely to be more important in cases of proprietary drug products, than in the case of other merchandise.
In the case of standard, widely available ethical drugs, the situation is much the same. Brand preference is somewhat more important, and products of long established ethical drug firms, which enjoy a high reputation for the quality of their products, are able to command premium prices. There are practical limits to the amount of the premium which can be charged. The history of the industry indicates that once a drug becomes generally available to manufacturers, numerous alternative products are offered and prices tend to fall until they reflect only a modest mark-up over actual cost of production. As a drug becomes widely available, manufacturers usually stop promoting it aggressively and concentrate on promoting their more exclusive lines. This reduces the general costs of sale and distribution of the particular drug.
Regardless of what conclusions may be reached in respect of such matters, the fact which makes high prices possible is the patent control exercise over such drug. The clear intention of the special provisions of the Canadian patent law, is that this situation should not obtain. However, advantage has not been taken of these provisions, and the drug industry in Canada is, for all practical purposes, operating under conditions determined by the patent law of the United States.
Patent controlled drugs are imported into Canada by a few small firms, other than United States companies, generally classified as foreign, without any licence arrangements with the Canadian patent holders. The basic fact is, that such importations are made, and that importing firms offer dosage forms of such drugs at lower prices than the equivalent products offered by the patent holders.
To date, the availability of such products does not appear to have had any significant effect on the prices charged by the firm holding patents, except to a very limited extent in the case of some institutional buyers. This is due to a controversy which has raged and continues to rage about the quality of the imported products, and the products of small

firms. Until doctors generally are satisfied as to the quality of such products, their impact on the market and on the prices of established brand name products will continue to be slight. This situation, of course, would be entirely different if such drugs were available to all manufacturers.
Would the hon. member tell me the difference between generic and brand name drugs?
I did not understand the question.
What is the difference between generic and brand name drugs?
There is no difference.
Forget the malarkey, and tell me what the difference is.

As I said before, there is no difference between a generic and brand name drug, in so far as the drug itself is concerned. It is simply the same as one person calling a box of material Rinso, while someone else calls it soap flakes.
That is the worst malarkey I have ever heard in this house. The hon. member does not know what he is talking about.
Mr. Chairman, the reference to soap came to my mind when the hon. member rose to ask me a question.
All this C.C.F. malarkey is the same. I asked the hon. member a question, and he has not answered it.
You received your answer although you may not be able to appreciate or understand it.
I appreciated it.
If you wish me to go further I shall.
Just tell me what the difference is.
Order. The hon. member for Skeena has the floor, and until he yields it for a question by sitting down, I ask the hon. member for Yorkton to remain in his place.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could use another example to illustrate the difference, using a product for which the hon. member may have use later on. One brand name of a product is Bayer aspirin, and the generic name is acetylsalicylic acid. They are the same thing, but one is the generic term and the other the brand name.
How many grains are there in an aspirin? How many grains are there in a Bayer aspirin?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There are no grains at all, there is acetylsalicylic acid.
Order.
Now that the hon. and noisy member has gone behind the curtains, perhaps I can proceed.
I am back.

Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that the hon. member will need a whole box of aspirins, or perhaps one of the more powerful chemicals, tomorrow morning.
As I said, there is very little price competition at the retail level, and that which does exists is chiefly in respect of proprietary and sundry drug products; tooth paste, and things of that nature. Apart from a very few discount drug outlets, most Canadian drugs stores sell their ethical drug products-drugs on prescriptions-at the manufacturers' suggested resale price, as a matter of course. This appears to be due firstly to the practice of the manufacturers in basing all trade prices on the listed or suggested resale price, and the acceptance of this price by pharmacists as the only proper selling price. Second, this is due to the pressure exerted by certain pharmacists' associations and their members to maintain certain price levels.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to go further in this discussion, but I think what I have said sums up what I have said on previous occasions in respect of this item, as well as what I said during the last session in respect of an item in the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I feel the comments and conclusions which I have presented fairly well meet the conclusions arrived at by the director of the combines investigation branch following extensive research and investigation into this particular field. I suggest also that, to the extent it is possible to analyse the wealth of material that was presented to the Kefauver committee, similar conclusions were reached by that committee in respect of this situation, except with reference to the control by patents and sales tax regarding comparable prices paid to importers.
I feel similar conclusions were also arrived at by the United States federal trade commission as contained in the report of that commission, to which I referred earlier. I do not have that report now, as I gave it to Hansard and it has not been returned.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I express the hope that an inquiry into this very important field will not be delayed, but will be undertaken with the greatest dispatch. I understand the combines investigation branch, and the restrictive trade practices commission, will deal only with selling and pricing policies of
Supply-Justice
certain pharmaceutical houses in respect of certain types of drugs. These were the words used in the annual report by the director of research and investigation, but not the words which appear in the document which I was prevented from reading a while ago.
But this is only one phase of the drug industry, Mr. Chairman. I think the minister and his colleagues should take this under consideration and advisement and also take some steps to deal with it. There is ample room for additional study in some other related fields, for instance, in the field of the physiological and psychological effect upon an individual who may be taking certain of the so-called tranquillizers. What about the medical effect on him? This is something which is not thoroughly understood by doctors themselves. They are discovering new things as each day goes by.
These are questions which have been raised by eminent people in the medical profession and by writers in this particular field. What about the effect on the individual of the so-called multiple vitamins? They take a number of them and put them together. What about the effect on the individual of the maxing up of different types of drugs into one tablet? These are things which I appreciate come more directly under the Department of National Health and Welfare, as well as the question of the ethical drug industry advertising directly to doctors. I think this is something that I can mention in passing because it has a relationship with the drug industry.
As I understood the minister earlier, he said that they were keeping this matter under review to see what possible action could be taken after studying the statement of evidence, or whatever it is called. The minister works very closely with the Minister of National Health and Welfare on the question of narcotic drugs and their effect and in the prosecution of offenders, together with the treatment of people who are addicted. As I say, this is another field in which the Minister of Justice and the Minister of National Health and Welfare can work together very well. They should look into the activities of the drug industry from all points of view and their effect upon the consumer, the medical profession and illnesses. I submit that not only are the selling and pricing policies of immediate concern but the question of advertising of the ethical industry directly to doctors, and the question of the physiological and psychological effects of compounded drugs and new drugs on the individual who takes them.
Perhaps I should close my remarks on this particular phase of the matter and make

Supply-Justice
just one more comment about another subject at the risk of incurring the wrath of the Minister of Veterans Affairs but I think I must do this.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Give some other members a chance.

Recently there has been a fair amount of publicity attached to activities of certain companies in the province of Quebec. While I think this is a sort of minor part of it all-I do not wish to play up what is taking place on the political scene in Quebec-yet it is from a certain activity there that this information comes. I think there is ample material for investigation or study by the combines branch to see just what is going on.
Evidence was presented to the royal commission in Quebec to the effect, for argument's sake, that Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation was paying a rake-off or a kickback of $10 on a ton of steel. I am not concerned at this time about who got the money or whether it was illegal to pay kick-backs and so on, but I am concerned with the question of kick-backs. Dosco has been prosecuted and fined once already for price-fixing under the Combines Investigation Act, along with Stelco and one or two other companies, that had subsidiary companies. As I say, this is a company which has been prosecuted and fined on one occasion for price-fixing. I wonder whether the combines investigation branch should look very carefully into whether kick-backs or rake-offs of $10 a ton, as it is said Dosco paid, have been used to enhance the position of Dosco within the industry and to ensure that price competition did not have its full play? This is something which I think should be inquired into very carefully.
There are certain other things from the corporate moral point of view that we should look at. I am wondering whether it is morally correct for Dominion Steel and Coal Company to receive subsidies from the federal treasury and then take part of those subsidies and channel them back into the Union Nationale party coffers in another province?
As I say, this is another matter which perhaps is not of concern here. There is also attached to it the question of whether these rake-offs are really a charge against the operations of the company and are reflected in less income tax being paid into the federal treasury. Armco Drainage and Metal Products of Canada Limited is another company that has been mentioned as paying phony commissions or rake-offs to the extent of $1,200. We must remember that Armco Drainage and Metal Products of Canada Limited is another company that was prosecuted and

fined under the Combines Investigation Act not so long ago. Brandram-Henderson is another company that was mentioned. The reference there was that this company was paying phony commissions of $1.50 a gallon on luminous paint for sidewalk and street markings, and so on. The combines branch has an obligation to look into this question of rake-offs or kick-backs or the paying of phony commissions in order to get certain contracts from the provincial government of Quebec. There should be an inquiry to learn whether the payment of these phony salesmen's commissions or kick-backs, or whatever you want to call them, was not in fact a device used to limit or prevent competition and to ensure that the companies mentioned and others who were involved in this were not using it as a means to get into a monopolistic position and eliminate competition in that particular field.
The other day the minister said he did not want to get involved in the political picture in Quebec. From the point of view of the activities of the Combines Investigation Act I think this is something which requires very serious study and investigation, and I am sure the minister will bring these comments to the attention of the director if he himself has not already noticed these things in the press and undertaken some preliminary inquiry.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
173. Bankruptcy Act administration, $118,770.

I should like to say a few
words on this item which has to do with the administration of the Bankruptcy Act. I am inclined to do it owing to an experience of some years ago. I became very interested in the administration of the Bankruptcy Act and even at that time I was convinced that there was room for a great deal of improvement to protect creditors of the companies going into bankruptcy. As a matter of fact, at the request of a number of creditors at a creditors meeting I was appointed a special inspector to deal with certain aspects of bankruptcy because I had some knowledge of the physical assets and circumstances surrounding the bankruptcy of the company. I must say that it was that experience over a period of two or three years that caused me to become quite interested in the administration of the act and aware of the necessity for some improvements and amendments in the administration. I am not going to deal with the circumstances of that day but I am particularly inclined to raise the question again because of a rash of bankruptcies that occurred in the southeastern portion of British Columbia, particularly since world war II.

Bankruptcies in the lumbering industry have taken place under very suspicious circumstances. Generally speaking the companies were owned by United States citizens who operated in southeastern British Columbia, particularly in the Kootenays, for a period of one, two, three or four years and then went bankrupt. The owners or managers disappeared across the line and the merchants and other persons who were involved were, in ordinary language, left holding the bag. Mind you, this occurred repeatedly during the period when the forest industry was particularly flourishing. There did not seem to be much reason for this succession of bankruptcies, in one case repeated on three occasions by one man who at the present time is the owner of a company of considerable size south of the line.
I have made reference to this matter previously this session. In particular, I have referred to the bankruptcy of the Hilco Company Limited near Fruitvale which went bankrupt late last year. The owners disappeared across the line and in fact it was quite difficult to proceed with the bankruptcy and to ascertain who was responsible for the company later. Merchants and ordinary workmen were left holding the sack with very little knowledge of their rights and the responsibilities of officials and so on.
I have knowledge of the circumstances surrounding this case because I attended a meeting of the creditors. I did not do so because it was my personal responsibility. I was invited to attend the meeting because I had had some previous experience and had had a somewhat limited experience in the lumber industry. These people considered that I knew a little more about such matters than the average creditor involved. I attended with the idea of listening to the story of the creditors as to the circumstances surrounding this bankruptcy. This again leads me to believe that there must be amendments to the act to provide creditors with at least a rudimentary knowledge of the law-I am not suggesting that creditors can become as skilled in law as lawyers are-the responsibilities of the officers of the crown in administering the Bankruptcy Act, the sequence of procedures in administering the act and their rights in these matters.
I mentioned this matter briefly at the beginning of the session and the commercial attache to the United States embassy read my remarks in Hansard and very kindly telephoned me and told me they were very concerned about the information I had placed on the record. Later he came to my office and I discussed the circumstances with him and gave him the balance sheet and the other information that had been given to me. He
Supply-Justice
undertook to see that an investigation would be carried out in the United States and an investigation was in fact carried out in that country as to the operations of this company in the United States and in Canada. I am not going into the details. I have a letter here dealing with that. I can say that the report I received from this gentleman is not a credit to the company concerned.
That leads me to believe that there has to be some amendment to the act with respect to circumstances of this type where the owner has disappeared across the line. The minister will have an idea where the Lardeau district is because he likes to visit a beautiful district on occasion. I remember one case where a company had operated there for some months. The owner was able to get the men to work without wages for two months with the idea that he wanted to increase his capital so that he could expand. The company was shipping lumber to Nelson from where it went south on the Great Northern to the international boundary.
These men worked Saturdays and Sundays in an effort to assist the owner, but when the last trainload of lumber went out by rail and then by barge the owner went with it. He told the men that he would be back on Wednesday, that he had enough lumber now to get credit at the bank in order to be able to pay them. They waited until Wednesday and nothing happened. They waited until the following Saturday and then they began to make inquiries. The owner had this trainload of lumber shipped from Nelson over the Great Northern into the United States, and that was the last the men ever heard of it.
That circumstance has been repeated on a number of occasions in different forms. That is why I am particularly interested in amendments to the Bankruptcy Act, and if I heard the minister correctly yesterday I understood him to say that the department is giving consideration to amending the act. These repeated bankruptcies clearly indicate that some shady business goes on at times and that worthy creditors and workmen are not adequately protected. I wrote later to the superintendent of bankruptcy and received a letter from him in reply. He was quite concerned about this matter and I should like to quote part of his letter dated April 21, 1961. He said:
I have your letter of the 13th instant and enclosure the contents of which are noted. However, unfortunately, the Bankruptcy Act as now constituted does not seem to contain a remedy and I must confess that the solution is not immediately apparent. Should you have any suggestions, I shall be only too pleased to receive them and to give them due and proper consideration in conjunction with a study of the present provisions.

Supply-Justice
I frankly admit that I am not a lawyer and my suggestions are simply made on the basis of the experience of a layman with a number of these cases. I suggest that amendments are required to protect the public and creditors to a greater extent than is provided in the present act. I suggest that amendments are required to provide more severe penalties to restrain dishonest persons to a greater extent.
I suggest that in the administration of the act there is a necessity for permanent regional officers so that people will know where to go and so that someone will be available whose sole duty it is to administer the Bankruptcy Act in a certain area with a knowledge of the law.
I suggest that action be taken to provide that the minutes of creditors' meetings should not just be entered as minutes but that a stenographic report should be made by a court stenographer so that there will be an accurate record of the questions and answers. I also suggest that there should be something in the nature of an information booklet to give creditors of companies going into bankruptcy some general information as to how to proceed.
Six o'clock.

My final suggestion, and I will not be long-heavens above, I have sat here in patience for two days and I am trying to conclude in a few minutes. If it were not for the time factor and my sympathy for the minister I could go on at much greater length. My final suggestion is that there should be amendments to provide for situations where a person who goes into bankruptcy goes across the line and is out of reach of the creditors. I noticed in the Canada Gazette recently the reappointment of the trustees in bankruptcy and there is one omission. There are no trustees appointed for the Kootenay district, east or west. In view of our history in this respect and the need for a trustee, I suggest that until the law is amended the minister give consideration to the appointment of a trustee in the Kootenay district to serve that area. That is all I have to say.

I want to thank the hon. member for his remarks and tell him that we will give consideration to the points he has raised.

to carry items 173 and 174 so that we could start with the penitentiaries branch the next time these estimates are before the committee.
Shall vote 173 carry?
